plos-pone-0004867:
Kun Wang led a team that used brain scans to study mind wandering for PLOS ONE in 2009. Mind wandering, also called daydreaming, fills a large share of waking life. Yet what it is for was still not clear. Some think the brain uses quiet moments to replay and sort recent events, much as it does in sleep, but proof from scans was thin at the time.

The team scanned people at rest and found a network that turns on in such moments. That network is the same one tied to memory replay. Its activity fits the idea that daydreams help the brain store what just happened. Rest, in this view, is work time for memory.
plos-pone-0005467:
Koji Taniguchi and colleagues tested a way to grow new blood vessels in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Proteins called Sproutys put a brake on signals that tell tissues to branch and grow. The team asked what that brake does to blood vessel growth after blood flow is blocked.

Using gene methods and short RNA tools in mice, they eased the brake off. Vessel growth improved, and tissue hit by poor blood flow fared better. The result points to a possible treatment path for limbs and organs starved of blood, though much more testing would be needed.
plos-pone-0005567:
John Wares and co-authors built a family tree of shallow-water barnacles in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Barnacles of the genus Chthamalus live high on rocky shores in a harsh zone between the tides. Classic studies of competition between species used these animals.

Using several genes, the team mapped how the western hemisphere species are related. The tree was surprisingly shallow, meaning the species split recently. A clear family tree lets ecologists re-read the classic competition studies with the true relationships in hand. A recent split also means that shore ecologists may be comparing species that still look and act much alike.
plos-pone-0005667:
Peter Tickle, Robert Nudds, and Jonathan Codd measured breathing bones across bird species in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Breathing must supply oxygen at the rate the body burns it. Birds have small bony struts called uncinate processes on their ribs, which help the muscles that drive breathing.

The team compared the length of those struts with each species' resting metabolic rate. Longer struts went with higher rates, matching the idea that the struts help the chest work harder. The link shows how skeleton shape tracks the demands of flight and daily life in birds.
plos-pone-0005767:
Jingjing Gu and co-authors scanned thoroughbred horse genomes in 2009 for marks of strong selection. Thoroughbreds were bred hard for racing speed from a small founder pool. That intense, recent selection reshaped their bodies for elite performance.

Selection leaves stretches of DNA unusually uniform across the breed. The team hunted those stretches to find genes behind athletic traits. Such genes may govern muscle, heart, or lung performance. The scan also shows the cost of narrow breeding, in lost variation. Results can inform both horse care and the biology of exercise capacity.
plos-pone-0005867:
Daniel Larocque and co-authors reported in 2009 that two RNA-binding proteins both halt cell growth and help wrap nerve fibers in myelin. Mice with the quaking mutation have poorly compacted myelin in brain and nerves. Their qk gene makes several protein forms that sit in different cell compartments.

Two of those forms, QKI-6 and QKI-7, blocked proliferation and promoted Schwann cell myelination in the team's tests. Schwann cells wrap peripheral nerves; their failure causes neuropathies. Linking specific QKI forms to wrapping gives myelin research defined targets. It also helps explain the quaking mouse's tremor at the molecular level.
plos-pone-0006467:
Christine Clay, Erin Lehmer, Stephen St. Jeor, and colleagues tested two rival ideas about diversity and disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. Species diversity is proposed to strongly affect how common a pathogen is. The dilution effect predicts that more diversity lowers pathogen spread, since many hosts are poor carriers. The amplification effect predicts the opposite: more diversity means more spread.

The team used Sin Nombre virus, a rodent-borne virus, and the rodent communities that carry it. Field data let them weigh which prediction fits. The answer matters for how land use and species loss may change disease risk. It also tests a theory used far beyond this one virus.
plos-pone-0006567:
Virginie Ropars, Gilles Despouy, Marc-Henri Stern, and colleagues studied a cancer protein's binding in PLOS ONE in 2009. The TCL1A oncoprotein plays key roles in several B and T cell malignancies. Lacking enzymatic activity, TCL1A's transforming action was linked to its partners. The team examined its interaction with IkB, the inhibitor of NF-kB.

Their title reports that TCL1A interacts directly with the NF-kB inhibitor. Binding the inhibitor could free NF-kB, a powerful survival signal for blood cells. That would explain how TCL1A drives leukemia without being an enzyme. The direct interaction gives drug designers a defined interface to target.
plos-pone-0009467:
Matthew Cairns and colleagues ran a trial with infants in Tanzania, reported in PLOS ONE in 2010. Babies can be given malaria drugs at set visits even when they are not sick. That plan aims to stop malaria before it starts. It was not clear how long each dose keeps a baby safe. Three drug plans were compared in the trial.

The team tracked how long protection lasted after treatment under each plan. They also weighed whether the drugs work by stopping new infections or by clearing ones already there. Knowing the length of protection helps planners choose drugs as old ones lose power. It also guides when doses should be given.
plos-pone-0009567:
Jennifer Bain and co-authors studied brain injury in young rodents in PLOS ONE in 2010. Babies born early, and those whose brains lose blood flow, often suffer white matter damage. White matter is the brain's wiring, and harm there can cause lasting disability. In the newborn brain, a zone called the SVZ makes cells for that wiring. The team tested a signal protein, TGF beta 1, in a model of this injury.

The protein pushed precursor cells to make too many astrocytes, a support cell type. That overproduction came at the cost of the wiring cells the brain needs. The finding names a lever in newborn brain damage. Adjusting it could one day help shield preterm infants.
plos-pone-0009667:
Nazare Pereira-Rodrigues and co-authors tested a coating for growing liver cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lab devices often use a silicone called PDMS as a surface for cells. A coating of parylene-C can change that surface's chemistry. The team grew hepatocarcinoma cells, a liver cancer type, on coated and uncoated PDMS. They compared the cells' shape and activity on each surface.

The coating changed how the cancer cells spread, stuck, and behaved. So surface chemistry alone can steer tumor cell behavior in the dish. That insight helps design better lab models of liver cancer. Engineered surfaces may become tools for testing drugs under more lifelike conditions.
plos-pone-0010467:
Shigeo Hasegawa and co-workers traced a pain pathway from nerve injury to a receptor in the spine for PLOS ONE in 2010. Neuropathic pain follows damage to peripheral nerves and resists most treatments, even opioids. The team had earlier found that nerve injury switches on an enzyme in immune-like cells of the spinal cord area. That enzyme helps make a signal called PAF. They asked what PAF's receptor does next.

The receptor drove production of inflammatory signals in the dorsal root ganglion. It also contributed to abnormal pain sensitivity to touch in rodents. A named receptor is a possible drug target for pain that opioids miss. The study links one injury to one molecular chain, step by step.
plos-pone-0010567:
Hyunchul Kim and co-workers compared mutation styles in a bacterium for PLOS ONE in 2010. Change linked to transcription diversified proteins faster, they found. During transcription, one DNA strand sits exposed and unprotected. Exposed bases mutate more readily than paired ones. Those extra mutations cluster where genes are read. The team asked whether that bias beats random mutation at creating protein variety in E. coli.

Their answer was yes: transcription-linked mutation raised protein diversity more effectively. Variety is the raw material of evolution, so its sources matter. A bias tied to gene use could speed adaptation where it counts. That idea tweaks standard views of random mutation. The study uses a model bacterium to test an evolutionary principle.
plos-pone-0010667:
Elena Biagi and colleagues compared gut microbes of older adults and centenarians, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gut community changes as the body ages, along with diet, immunity, and the gut itself. People past one hundred offer an extreme case worth studying.

The team profiled microbes and inflammation markers in seniors and in the very old. Centenarians carried a distinct mix, with more of some groups tied to inflammation. Their blood markers of inflammation also ran higher. Long life, it seems, can coexist with a more inflamed gut. That nuance tempers simple claims that one ideal gut mix guarantees healthy aging.
plos-pone-0010767:
Masayuki Nitta and colleagues proposed an indirect attack on a deadly brain tumor, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Glioblastoma grows fast and resists most treatment. Many of these tumors lean on a growth receptor called EGFR. Drugs blocking EGFR have helped far less than hoped, so the team looked for a weakness the receptor itself creates.

EGFR-driven cells live with high oxidative stress, a rust-like strain inside the cell. Blocking a repair enzyme, PARP1, pushed that strain past what tumor cells could bear. Normal cells, under less stress, were spared. The tactic turns the tumor's own driving signal into its fatal flaw.
plos-pone-0010867:
Chengzhang Liao, Yiqi Luo, Changming Fang and co-authors published this forest analysis in PLOS ONE in 2010. Planting forests is widely promoted as a way to soak up carbon and slow climate change. The authors asked how much carbon planted forests actually store compared with the natural forests they often replace.

They combined results from dozens of paired-site studies around the world. Total carbon stored in plants and soil was lower in plantations by more than a quarter, and plantations also showed less litterfall, slower soil breathing, thinner fine roots, and poorer soil nutrients. Liao and colleagues do not dismiss planting, but they warn that a plantation is not a carbon copy of a natural forest. Climate plans that swap one for the other may overstate the benefit.
plos-pone-0010967:
Argel Aguilar-Valles, Cecilia Flores and Giamal Luheshi published this rat study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Infection during pregnancy raises the offspring's later risk of schizophrenia, and disrupted dopamine development is a suspected link. The authors focused on a side effect of any infection: a drop in the mother's blood iron, which the developing fetal brain needs to build dopamine neurons.

They used a rat model where a local injury triggers whole-body inflammation without any germ. In it, they tested whether extra iron for the mother protected the pups' dopamine function. That was judged by behavior after drug challenges in adulthood. Aguilar-Valles and colleagues isolate iron shortage from the infection itself, a distinction earlier models blurred. If low iron is the culprit, a simple supplement during pregnancy could reduce a serious psychiatric risk.
plos-pone-0011067:
Elena Shumay, Joanna Fowler and Nora Volkow published this brain genetics analysis in PLOS ONE in 2010. The dopamine transporter recycles the brain chemical dopamine. It is tied to many mental conditions and traits. Yet decades of studies on its gene have given mixed results. The authors re-examined the gene's architecture for features that could explain that confusion.

Their broad computer analysis argues the gene carries odd features that make it highly regulable. Its activity can vary a lot between brain regions and states. Epigenetic control may be part of that. Such flexibility would let the same gene produce different effects in different people and contexts. Shumay and team propose that this elusiveness is a property of the gene itself. Studies must measure its regulation, not just its spelling.
plos-pone-0011167:
Valera, Isaacs, Kawakami and colleagues compared bone signals in PLOS ONE in 2010. Two bone growth proteins can pair up as matching twins or as a mixed pair. The team tested which form best drives human embryonic stem cells to develop into more mature cell types.

The mixed pair worked better than either matching pair on its own. That synergy means labs can guide stem cells with lower doses or stronger effect. Better control over cell fate is a core need in stem cell work. The result improves protocols that aim to grow tissues for research and future repair.
plos-pone-0011267:
Gomes, Wee, Khan and colleagues classified dengue patients by gene data in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dengue fever ranges from mild illness to life threatening shock, and doctors need early signs of severity. The team used gene expression patterns from patients and a machine learning method to sort cases.

Their classifier could separate patients in ways that match disease severity. An early warning tool like this could guide who needs close hospital watch during outbreaks. That triage saves lives when wards are overwhelmed. The study shows how patient gene data and computing can combine into a practical forecast.
plos-pone-0011367:
Lauren Woodard and colleagues checked in 2010 how lab technique itself can change results in a mouse liver cancer model. Researchers grow liver tumors in mice by injecting DNA into the liver under pressure, often adding an enzyme that stitches the DNA into the genome. The model carries an activated cancer gene, but the delivery steps might also shape how fast tumors appear.

The team varied the injection and enzyme steps and timed how long tumors took to form. Timing shifted with the method, showing that technique is an active variable, not a neutral delivery truck. Cancer modelers who ignore that variable risk comparing tumors that differ for the wrong reason. The paper is a practical warning: standardize delivery, report it fully, and read latency claims with the method in mind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1267:
On 17 July 1945, the summit's opening day, the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum. A staff paper from day one set the armed forces' view before the team as the talks began. The chiefs' office worked in step with the conference from its first hours.

Opening-day papers framed the questions as the soldiers saw them. Later notes would react to the bargaining; this one preceded it. That gives it a clean value: the military view before the trades began. It is the first of the long chiefs-of-staff run in this part of the volume, and it sets the tone for the rest.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1367:
Edwin Wilson, the American ambassador in Turkey, cabled the acting secretary of state on 19 July 1945. Turkey had stayed out of the war until its final months, then joined the winning side. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Ankara's post mattered because Turkey guards the straits between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, a passage Russia had coveted for ages. Soviet pressure on Turkey was rising in 1945, and Wilson reported from the front of that squeeze. His cable shows how a regional strain reached Washington during Potsdam, where the straits question sat on the leaders' own table as well.
frus-1945-50-intel-d67:
McCormack wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 7 January 1946, as the intelligence settlement reached its final fortnight. McCormack's research and intelligence office at State stood to gain or lose much by the outcome. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

A special assistant writing to his secretary at such a moment usually pleads a last point or reports a last danger. McCormack had built the State office from the OSS's research branch in four months, and its fate hung on the directive being drafted. Readers should read his January papers as the work of a man near the finish line. His own place beyond it was growing less sure. The new system, when it came, owed his office much and kept it little.
frus-1945-50-intel-d167:
A letter from the President’s Chief of Staff (Leahy) reached the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (Hoover) on 4 September 1946. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 167 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. At the time, a new National Intelligence Authority oversaw central intelligence, and the Central Intelligence Group did its daily work.

Writers chose a letter when they wanted a stance to count. The text gives the sender's side in full. Many of the big fights of these years can be followed letter by letter. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d267:
On 26 April 1948, the Executive Secretary (Souers) sent a memorandum to the Members of the National Security Council. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 267 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The Cold War was turning harder that year, and the new Council and CIA were being tested by it week by week.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d367:
On 14 February 1949, the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination (Wisner) sent a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. The State Department prints it as document 367 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1861-d67:
Writing on 12 August 1861, William H. Seward kept up his steady stream of letters to Charles Francis Adams. The letter is document 67 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Mid August found the Union cause in Europe at a low point. Seward kept his letters short, plain, and free of despair. For Adams, each such page was both an order and a sign of trust. Their steady tone did much to hold Britain's respect through a bleak season. Adams answered each order in turn, which kept the London file in neat pairs. Neat pairs in the file let readers trace each point from order to answer.
frus-1861-d167:
On 22 June 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Carl Schurz as Spain set its neutral course. The letter is document 167 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's June letter reached toward Madrid as Spain set its neutral course. Cuba made Spain a sea power near the American coast. Clear orders to Schurz helped keep Spanish ports and Cuban waters from aiding the South by stealth. Spanish cruisers and Cuban ports both fell under the watch Schurz had to keep. The watch he kept ran from the court's doors to the docks of Cadiz. The watch ran from court doors to Cadiz docks.
frus-1861-d267:
The home office spoke to James Shepherd Pike on 11 November 1861, through a letter from Seward. It stands as Document 267 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It belongs to the autumn of the war's first year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d67:
The home office spoke to Charles Francis Adams on 20 May 1862, through a letter from Seward. It stands as Document 67 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The letter comes from the spring of 1862, a year into the war, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d167:
Document 167, dated 25 October 1862, is one of three Seward dispatches to London printed under that date in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. All three went to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain.

A cluster of same-day letters usually means a mail steamer was about to sail and the Department cleared its desk at once. Orders, war news, and copies of other papers could all leave on the same tide. For historians, clusters like this one mark the rhythm of transatlantic diplomacy, driven by ship schedules as much as by events. British backing for the South would have brought Richmond credit, ships, and fresh hope at once.
frus-1862-d267:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William L. Dayton on 16 April 1862, a day after his previous Paris dispatch. The letter is Document 267 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Two letters in two days from the Secretary usually means fresh news to send or a point to underline twice. The spring mails to Paris carried the Union's case at a moment when New Orleans was about to fall to a Union fleet. That prize, a great port and cotton outlet, spoke loudly in Europe, and Seward made sure his envoy could speak to it. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived.
frus-1862-d367:
Document 367, dated 31 May 1862, is a memorandum of a conversation between Henri Mercier. The French minister in Washington, and Secretary of State William H. Seward. Such memoranda were written up after talks to fix what had been said.

A recorded conversation differs from a letter: it captures diplomacy done aloud, with questions, hints, and warnings that formal notes avoid. Memoranda in this file are among its most revealing papers. This one comes from the weeks after Mercier's Richmond trip, when face-to-face talk between the two men carried more weight than paper. The French legation's notes were written in French and printed here in the Department's English.
frus-1862-d467:
George Perkins Marsh, the American minister in Turin, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 6 January 1862. It is Document 467 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the first Italian paper in the file.

Marsh opened the year reporting from a kingdom barely ten months old, where the American war was followed with fellow feeling. Italy's leaders had just fought to unite their own country and saw the Union's cause in that light. His early report gave Washington a measure of Italian sympathy and of the new kingdom's standing among the powers. The letter starts a file that stands out in the volume for its genuine cordiality.
frus-1862-d567:
Henry Shelton Sanford reported from Brussels to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 August 1862. The dispatch is Document 567 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress with the annual message.

Late August 1862 was a low season for the Union, and Sanford's reports that summer did not hide it. From Belgium he could watch French policy hardening in Mexico and British opinion swinging with the battle news. He also pursued his standing hunt for Confederate agents and purchases in Europe. Seward needed such reporting most when times were worst, and Sanford supplied it without varnish. The letter belongs to the hard summer file that precedes the turn at Antietam.
frus-1862-d667:
On 7 August 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a formal note to the ministers for foreign affairs of Japan. It is document 667 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, the last of his direct notes to the court in this file. Robert H. Pruyn was by then running the American legation.

Notes sent over an envoy's head were rare, and they marked points Washington wanted stated in its own voice. This one belongs with the two earlier notes to the same ministers, in 1861 and in March 1862. Together the three show a young tie kept up by set forms, long waits, and great care on both sides.
frus-1863p1-d67:
Charles Francis Adams dated this dispatch 30 January 1863 and sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 67 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Adams wrote at the end of a full month of London work. His January mail had covered the freedom edict's welcome in Britain and the cabinet's watchful calm. Reports like this one let Seward weigh whether the tide across the sea ran for or against the Union. The dispatch is a quiet, workmanlike piece of the file, of the kind the whole record is built from.
frus-1863p1-d167:
For the first of his three letters of 24 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward from London. Three Adams letters in the volume bear the date, and two Seward letters share it too. Adams was the American minister in London; this letter is document 167 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Five sheets in the file bear 24 April, a peak day for the exchange. Adams's three took the London heads in turn: talks, yards, and press. This one opens his set. The pile for one date shows both capitals at full work on the same brief, in the spring the ship fight turned.
frus-1863p1-d267:
From his London post on 21 August 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 267 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d367:
In Washington on 20 January 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 367 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Lyons was the man Seward had to persuade, warn, or answer in person in Washington. Notes to him carried the American side of each dispute between the two governments. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d467:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 17 April 1863 letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d567:
On 16 June 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington wrote to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the early summer of 1863.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d667:
From Charles Francis Adams, America's minister in London to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State: a letter dated 19 November 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0000067:
Zachary Lippman, Bruce May, Cristy Yordan, and their team published this paper in PLOS Biology in 2003. It studies transposons, the DNA stretches that can move around a genome. Cells keep them quiet with chemical marks called methylation and with small RNAs that guide the silencing.

The puzzle is how a cell passes that quiet state to the next generation. The authors show that the routes for keeping marks and for handing them down are not the same. Small interfering RNA and changes to histones, the spools DNA wraps around, play separate parts. The work sharpens the picture of how genomes stay stable while their jumping genes stay under control.
plos-pbio-0020167:
June Yao, Tu Cam Le, Claudine H. Kos, and their team explained a genetic kidney disease in PLOS Biology in 2004. The disease, FSGS, scars the kidney's filters and can end in kidney failure. Some families pass it down through a faulty gene for α-actinin-4, a protein that helps hold cell shape.

The study shows the faulty protein clumps together and breaks down too fast, wrecking the cells that form the filter. That gives a clear chain from gene to disease. Clear chains are what treatment design needs. If clumping is the problem, drugs that keep the protein stable or clear the clumps become plausible goals for this inherited form of kidney failure.
plos-pbio-0020367:
Hannah E. Volkman, Hilary Clay, Dana Beery, and their team studied tuberculosis in zebrafish in PLOS Biology in 2004. In TB, immune cells wall off the bacteria in ball-like clusters called granulomas. The team found a bacterial factor that helps those clusters form and grow.

That flips a common view. Granulomas were long cast as the host's defense alone, yet here the germ itself promotes them. The clusters may shelter bacteria as much as they trap them. If so, blocking the bacterial factor could help the host clear infection. Zebrafish larvae, clear enough to watch live, make the process visible in a way mammal studies cannot match.
plos-pone-0000067:
Rajesh Khanna, Qi Li, and Elise F. Stanley analyzed a nerve ending protein complex in PLOS ONE in 2006. At the synapse, where one nerve cell passes signals to the next, proteins must be pulled back inside after use. Synaptotagmin 1 anchors a complex that runs that retrieval, called endocytosis.

Their fractional recovery analysis measures how much of the complex can be drawn back into action after stress. Precise numbers for recovery help model how synapses keep up during heavy use without running dry. Fast, faithful recycling is what lets nerve signals stay reliable at high rates. The study gives synaptic physiology a careful measure of a key machine.
plos-pone-0000167:
Long-Jun Wu, Shanelle W. Ko, Hiroki Toyoda, and colleagues published this neuroscience paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It studies mice with the GluR5 gene knocked out, removing one type of receptor for the brain signal glutamate. The authors focus on the amygdala, the brain region tied to fear and anxiety.

The knockout mice showed more anxiety-like behavior and stronger synaptic responses in the amygdala. Linking one receptor to both changes ties a molecule to a mood-related trait. The work helps map how glutamate signaling shapes anxiety, a connection of interest for treating anxiety disorders.
plos-pone-0000267:
Jaspreet Singh Jaggi, Erik Henke, Surya V. Seshan, and colleagues published this cancer therapy paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Alpha particles are heavy, short-range radiation that can kill cells precisely. The authors use alpha-particle treatment aimed at a tumor's blood vessels, selectively depleting the vasculature. The treatment also brings about vascular normalization, a brief window where remaining vessels work better.

Starving a tumor by cutting its blood supply is an established strategy; doing it with targeted radiation is sharper. The normalization window can let other drugs reach the tumor more effectively. The study explores that combination logic in a cancer model.
plos-pone-0000367:
Nitika Pant Pai and colleagues evaluated a rapid HIV test in rural India, publishing their work in PLOS ONE in 2007. Instead of drawing blood, the test uses fluid from the mouth, which is easier and less painful to collect. The team checked three things: how accurate the test is, whether it can work in rural clinics, and whether clients prefer it.

Fast, simple testing matters where lab access is limited and many infections go undiagnosed. A mouth-fluid test that people accept could bring screening to places that blood-based programs reach poorly. The study weighs test performance against real-world use, a balance that decides whether a good test actually helps in the field.
plos-pone-0000467:
Matthew D. Smith and colleagues folded an artificial protein and studied what made the fold stable, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The protein is non-biological, designed rather than evolved. The team drew structural insights into its evolution. They focused on surface residues, the amino acids on the protein's outside. Those residues proved important in optimizing its fold.

Designers often focus on a protein's core, but the surface also decides whether a chain settles into one shape. Lessons from a designed protein's trial-and-error improvement read like a compressed evolution experiment. They feed back into protein engineering, where stable, well-folded designs are the starting point for new enzymes and materials.
plos-pone-0000567:
Maren N. Vitousek and colleagues measured the price female choice exacts in a lekking lizard, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. In a lek, males gather to display and females visit to choose mates, gaining no resources, only genes. The team documented high costs of female choice in this system.

Choice can cost time, energy, and exposure to predators while a female compares males. If costs are high, females should be choosy only when the payoff is large, which shapes how the mating system evolves. Measuring the cost side of choice, not just its benefits, gives a fuller account of sexual selection in the wild.
plos-pone-0000667:
David Emerson, Jeremy A. Rentz, Timothy G. Lilburn and co-authors described a new lineage of iron-eating bacteria in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bacteria that oxidize iron are tied to hydrothermal vents, where iron-rich fluids rise around underwater mountains called seamounts. For decades the evidence for these microbes came almost entirely from the mineral remains they leave behind.

Living members of this new proteobacterial lineage help build marine microbial mats, layered communities on surfaces. Naming the organisms behind the rusty mats turns geology into biology: their genes and growth can now be studied directly. Iron cycling shapes ocean chemistry, so the microbes doing it matter well beyond the vents.
plos-pone-0000767:
Hoorig Nassanian, Ana M. Sanchez, Alice Lo and colleagues streamlined a standard gene-silencing tool, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. RNA interference, mediated by small interfering RNA, silences genes after they are transcribed. Once inside target cells, siRNAs join the RNA-induced silencing complex, whose antisense strand guides it to matching RNA for destruction. Labs build DNA cassettes to produce siRNAs inside cells.

Their cassette uses a minimal H1 promoter, inverted for easier handling. The design eases exchange of both the promoter and the siRNA sequence. Tool papers rarely make headlines, but faster cassette building speeds every experiment that knocks a gene down to see what happens.
plos-pone-0000867:
Fabio Moroni, Lino Nobili, Giuseppe Curcio and colleagues recorded sleep activity inside the human hippocampus, in a 2007 PLOS ONE study. The hippocampus is a deep brain area tied to forming new memories of facts and events. Sleep is widely thought to help lock those memories in place.

Using stereo-EEG, fine electrodes placed inside the brain, the team watched how this area behaves across sleep. They set its activity beside activity in the outer cortex. Work of this kind is rare because it needs direct recordings from inside the human brain. It sharpens our picture of how sleep and memory fit together.
plos-pone-0000967:
Richard Edwards, Norman Davey and Denis Shields built a probabilistic tool for finding short working motifs in proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Short linear motifs are tiny stretches, three to ten building blocks, that do key jobs in cells. As few as two positions in a motif may matter, which makes them very hard to spot.

Their program, SLiMFinder, looks for motifs that appear more often than chance allows and that evolved independently in separate proteins. Convergent evolution, the same trick found twice, is strong evidence a motif is real. Better motif hunting expands the map of how proteins talk to each other.
plos-pone-0001067:
Jinshun Zhao, Vasu Punj, Hittu Matta and colleagues studied a viral protein that blocks its own virus's active phase, in PLOS ONE in 2007. KSHV is the herpesvirus behind Kaposi's sarcoma. Growing evidence ties disordered expression of its lytic genes, the genes of active copying, to tumor formation.

A viral protein called K13 blocks that lytic replication, the team report, and also deregulates viral and human interleukin-6, immune signals tied to growth. Their model suggests lytic slips help select clones that become tumors. A virus holding its own accelerator and brake helps explain the slow, patchy way this cancer develops.
plos-pone-0001167:
Wound healing requires cells to know when to multiply, move, and settle into new tissue. Srinivasulu Chigurupati and colleagues examined the Notch signaling pathway in that process, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Notch is a communication system between cells that is deeply involved in fate decisions during development.

The team used both animal and cell culture models, looking at the healing of full-thickness skin wounds. Their findings place Notch among the signals that coordinate repair. Knowing which pathways drive healing could eventually point to ways of helping wounds that heal slowly, a common problem in diabetes and old age.
plos-pone-0001267:
When oxygen returns to tissue that has been starved of it, the returning oxygen itself causes damage, a well-known problem in mammals. John Lighton and Pablo Schilman set out to study that reperfusion damage in an insect, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. A small, genetically well characterized animal model with reproducible, quantifiable damage was lacking.

The authors present the insect as such a model for oxygen reperfusion injury. In plain terms, they show the damage can be produced and measured in a convenient laboratory animal. That opens the genetics of reperfusion injury, relevant to heart attack and stroke care, to fast experimental study.
plos-pone-0001367:
Martha Hamblin, Marilyn Warburton, and Edward Buckler wrote a 2007 PLOS ONE study that compares two kinds of DNA markers in maize, or corn. One kind is short repeated DNA stretches. The other kind is single letter changes in the DNA code. Breeders use both kinds to judge how alike two corn plants are.

The authors weigh how well each marker type shows the spread and the family links in maize. They note that the two types change at unlike rates, so they can give unlike views of the same plants. Their results help breeders and gene banks pick the right test for the task at hand.
plos-pone-0001467:
Maja Trenner and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how the brain handles cues across the senses. Past work compared brain replies to targets that cues had flagged as right or wrong. Less was known about brain work in the gap between cue and target. The team recorded brain rhythms in that gap.

They found that wave patterns in the wait help set up the gain from a good cue. In short, the brain does key work before the target shows. That work spans senses, since the cue and target can be in unlike modes. The study helps explain how alertness is held over a brief wait.
plos-pone-0001567:
Daniel Macqueen and Ian Johnston wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE update on a muscle gene called MyoD in fish. MyoD is a master switch for making muscle in backboned animals. Some fish hold two or more copies of it, a legacy of past genome doublings. Other fish hold just one. The pair reviewed the full record across fish lines.

They set out a shared naming plan to keep the copies from being mixed up. Mixed names had bred false claims on which copy does what. A clean roster helps labs compare muscle growth across species. It also frames how gene copies split jobs after a doubling.
plos-pone-0001667:
Takeshi Hase, Yoshihito Niimura, and Tsuguchika Kaminuma compared the wiring of protein networks across evolution in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Proteins in a cell form a web of interactions. Such networks are scale-free, meaning a few hub proteins hold many links while most hold few. The authors focused on heterodimerization links, pairs where two different proteins bind.

They asked whether these links survive at the same rate across the yeast protein interaction network's history. Their answer, signaled in the title, is no: survival is non-uniform, with some link types lasting far longer than others. The full text gives the network data and the survival rates by link type. Uneven survival shows where natural selection guards the web most tightly.
plos-pone-0001767:
Ricardo Águas, Lisa J. White, Robert W. Snow, and their co-authors modeled malaria elimination in sub-Saharan Africa in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Plasmodium falciparum infections build clinical immunity gradually through repeated exposure. How that protection works at the gene level was not yet known. Its effects on spread patterns are strong and must enter any elimination plan.

The authors weigh the odds of wiping malaria out, given this built-up immunity. The full text gives the model, the transmission settings, and which areas look feasible. Immunity changes the math of elimination: as transmission falls, protection fades, which can set up rebounds. Plans that ignore this cycle risk declaring victory too early.
plos-pone-0001867:
Tiago Fleming Outeiro, Preeti Putcha, Julie E. Tetzlaff, and their co-authors watched a Parkinson's-linked protein clump inside living cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Misfolding, oligomerization, and fibrillization of alpha-synuclein are thought central to the onset and progression of Parkinson's disease and related disorders. Fibrillar alpha-synuclein is a major component of Lewy bodies, the clumps found in patient brains, but recent data implicated prefibrillar forms.

The team reports the formation of toxic oligomeric alpha-synuclein species in living cells: small assemblies, not the big fibrils, doing the damage. The full text gives the cell model and toxicity assays. If small oligomers are the toxic species, drug screens should target them rather than the visible end-stage clumps.
plos-pone-0001967:
Hans Rempel and co-authors studied a sticky protein that helps HIV spread between cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. HIV infection warps the immune system and changes which genes are active in monocytes, a white blood cell type in the blood. A scan of those genes found more sialoadhesin, also called CD169, on monocytes from infected people.

Sialoadhesin is a cell adhesion molecule, a kind of surface glue. The team report that when interferon raises its level on monocytes, the protein binds HIV and enhances how well the virus infects new cells. A host protein that helps the virus is a target worth blocking.
plos-pone-0002067:
Peter Southern and co-authors studied how a common yeast colonizes human surfaces, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Candida albicans lives at low level in most healthy people as a harmless commensal. Yet it holds a steady potential to expand and cause a spectrum of illnesses, from thrush to blood infection.

The team built lab models from human organ cultures kept alive outside the body, plus groups of primary human cells. With them, they watched how the yeast settles on mucosal surfaces, the wet linings of mouth, gut, and elsewhere. Models that mimic real tissue help test drugs and vaccines against this two-faced resident.
plos-pone-0002167:
Jing Huang, Lu Ma, Fei Yang, and co-authors reported weak points on plant chromosomes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In humans, fragile sites are stretches of chromosome that tend to show gaps or breaks when cells divide under stress. The team asked whether a like pattern exists in ryegrasses, plants in the genus Lolium.

They studied dividing cells from root tips. They focused on the regions carrying 45S ribosomal DNA, genes the cell uses heavily to build its protein factories. These regions showed up as gaps on the chromosomes, acting like fragile sites. The finding extends a mostly animal topic into plant genetics, with ryegrass as the test case.
plos-pone-0002267:
Nathalie Busso, Mahir Karababa, Massimo Nobile, and co-authors blocked an enzyme tied to inflammation and found a new pathway, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme NAMPT, also called visfatin, is the rate-limiting step in the cell's salvage route for making NAD, a molecule vital for energy use. Its levels rise during inflammation, and it had been flagged as a marker in acute lung injury.

By inhibiting NAMPT with a drug, the team showed its activity drives an inflammatory pathway linked to NAD levels. The link suggests that dialing down this one enzyme could cool inflammation in diseases where NAD balance runs off track.
plos-pone-0002367:
Mark Pogson, Mike Holcombe, Rod Smallwood, and co-authors added space to a model of a master immune switch, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Nature builds system behavior from local interactions among small parts, at cell, organ, and colony level alike. To understand the whole, models must capture those local rules. NF-kappaB is a transcription factor that switches on inflammation and immune genes.

Most models treated the cell as a well-mixed bag, ignoring where molecules sit. The team built an agent-based model that introduces spatial information into predictive NF-kappaB modeling. Putting molecules in space can change the predicted rhythm of the switch, and with it the cell's response to infection signals.
plos-pone-0002467:
Frøkjær-Jensen led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Christian Frøkjær-Jensen, Michael Ailion, Shawn R. Lockery, among others. Its subject is ammonium-Acetate Is Sensed by Gustatory and Olfactory Neurons in Caenorhabditis elegans. Caenorhabditis elegans chemosensation has been successfully studied using behavioral assays that treat detection of volatile and water soluble chemicals as separate senses.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002567:
Crossman and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Lisa C. Crossman, Santiago Castillo-Ramírez, Craig McAnnula, among others. Its subject is a Common Genomic Framework for a Diverse Assembly of Plasmids in the Symbiotic Nitrogen Fixing Bacteria. This work centres on the genomic comparisons of two closely-related nitrogen-fixing symbiotic bacteria, Rhizobium leguminosarum biovar viciae 3841 and Rhizobium etli CFN42.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002667:
Carlos del Fresno and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was monocytes from cystic fibrosis patients are locked in an LPS tolerance state: Down-Regulation of TREM-1 as putative underlying mechanism. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Carlos del Fresno, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. C ystic F ibrosis (CF) is an inherited pleiotropic disease that results from abnormalities in the gene that codes for the chloride channel. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002767:
Jan A. Hiss and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was domain organization of long signal peptides of Single-Pass integral membrane proteins reveals multiple functional capacity. The catalog record names Jan A. Hiss first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Targeting signals direct proteins to their extra - or intracellular destination such as the plasma membrane or cellular organelles. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002867:
John Neena and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on rapid assessment of avoidable blindness in india. Authorship is credited in the record to John Neena and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Rapid assessment of avoidable blindness provides valid estimates in a short period of time to assess the magnitude and causes of avoidable blindness. It goes on to note a further point. The study determined magnitude and causes of avoidable blindness in India in 2007 among the 50+ population. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002967:
Matthias Krauledat, Michael Tangermann, Benjamin Blankertz and co-authors aimed in 2008 to cut training time for brain-computer interfaces. EEG signals differ greatly between people and shift between sessions for the same person. That makes a stable interface hard, since the classic approach needs long calibration each time.

Their goal, stated in the title, is towards zero training. Published in PLOS ONE, the work tackles how an interface can adapt with little or no user-specific setup. Progress there matters for people who rely on such systems to communicate or control devices, where long setup is a real burden.
plos-pone-0003067: Maria Luisa Scattoni, Shruti Gandhy, Laura Ricceri and colleagues described vocalizations in the BTBR T+tf/J mouse in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The title calls the strain a mouse model of autism and its repertoire of vocalizations unusual. The catalog record supplies title, authors, and year, with an abstract snippet that repeats the title rather than adding findings. The article documents the range of calls these mice produce, material for researchers who use mouse vocal behavior to study social communication.
plos-pone-0003167:
Wieland H. Sommer, Antje Kraft, Sein Schmidt and colleagues ask how space is coded in the attention network in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Their question is to what extent the left and right visual fields are spatially coded in the dorsal frontoparietal network. In many studies with neglect patients, the left hemisphere favours the opposite field, while the right covers both fields.

The team study this dynamic spatial coding during a visual search task. Readers learn how the two sides of the brain divide attention across space. The work helps explain neglect after brain injury and how healthy search stays balanced.
plos-pone-0003267:
Warren D. Taylor and co-authors scan the brains of older adults with depression in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Which brain traits predict who gets better on antidepressant drugs was not well known for older patients. The team used a scan that maps white matter, the wiring that links brain areas, in patients on a twelve-week course of sertraline.

They test how frontal white matter structure relates to whether depression lifts. Readers see wiring treated as a clue to recovery, not just a backdrop. A fair clue of this kind could help doctors switch drugs sooner for those unlikely to improve.
plos-pone-0007467:
Ryan Klimczak and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on gene therapy for diseases of the retina. Many blinding retinal disorders have genetic causes, and tailored treatments for each are costly and limited. A shared feature is damage involving the retina's support cells, called Müller cells. The team sought a delivery virus that could reach those cells from inside the eye.

They engineered a new variant of adeno-associated virus for that job. Injected into the vitreous of rats, it transduced Müller cells efficiently and selectively. Selective delivery matters because treating the wrong cells wastes the therapy and risks harm. A carrier aimed this precisely could serve many retinal diseases at once. The study is a step toward practical gene therapy for inherited blindness.
plos-pone-0007567:
Katrin Schroeder and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how staph bacteria build biofilms on medical implants. Staphylococci are leading causes of implant infections. The critical step is colonization: bacteria gather into a three-dimensional film of cells and host material. The team characterized a surface protein of Staphylococcus aureus called SasC. They tested its part in holding the film together.

SasC helps the bacteria aggregate and accumulate into biofilms. A surface protein with that job sits exactly where drugs or antibodies could reach it. Each mapped piece of the biofilm machinery is a candidate target. Blocking clumping could keep implants clean without heavy antibiotics. The study adds one named component to the machinery behind some of the hardest hospital infections to cure.
plos-pone-0007667:
Mandë Holford and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on venom in a family of predatory sea snails. Terebrids, the auger snails, belong to a superfamily famous for neuroactive venoms. Finding new compounds starts with knowing which species carry a venom apparatus. Earlier work in the western Pacific showed some terebrids lack the apparatus entirely. The team matched the presence of the apparatus against a molecular family tree of Panamic species.

Venom equipment maps onto the phylogeny in an informative pattern. Knowing which branches carry the apparatus guides collectors to promising species. It also shows how the hunting toolkit evolved, gained here and lost there. Drug discovery from snails has already produced a painkiller from a cone snail relative. A good map shortens the search for the next one. The study weds evolution to pharmacology.
plos-pone-0007767:
Nils Homer and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It introduces BFAST, a tool for aligning DNA reads to a reference genome. New sequencing machines were producing billions of short reads. Resequencing a whole human genome depends on placing each read correctly and fast.

Alignment speed and accuracy both matter at that scale. BFAST was built to handle very large read sets against a large reference. Tools like this are the hidden plumbing of modern genomics. Every genome study since rests on aligners that can keep up with the machines.
plos-pone-0007867:
Yolanda Alvarez and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests a precise way to stop unwanted blood vessel growth in the eye. Such growth is a hallmark of diabetic retinopathy and age-related macular degeneration. Both diseases can end in blindness. Current treatments include laser surgery and targeted molecules.

The team aimed at one enzyme family, PI3 kinase, in the retina. Selective inhibition slowed retinal angiogenesis in their model. A more selective drug could spare healthy vessels while blocking harmful ones. The study marks PI3 kinase as a handle for future eye therapies.
plos-pone-0007967:
Anna Dongari-Bagtzoglou and colleagues gave the first close look at thrush films on living tissue in PLOS ONE in 2009. Candida albicans, a yeast, causes repeat infections of the gut and mouth lining. It was well known on plastic and steel, but not on the soft lining itself.

Films grown on mucosa turned out to have their own build and habits. That may explain why these infections return even after strong antifungal drugs: films shield the yeast within. Knowing how the film forms on real tissue helps the hunt for ways to break it apart.
plos-pone-0008067:
Kazutoshi Takahashi and colleagues grew human reprogrammed stem cells on feeders made from the same person in PLOS ONE in 2009. Such stem cells, called iPS cells, are adult cells rewound to a flexible state. For human care they must be grown without animal products, which can carry risk.

Feeder cells grown from the donor's own body gave the support the stem cells need with no foreign material. The self-supported setup brings lab-grown replacement tissue a step closer to the clinic. It also eases fears about hidden animal germs in cell therapy.
plos-pone-0008167:
Musa Jawara and colleagues tuned odor-baited mosquito traps in the Gambia in PLOS ONE in 2009. Traps that smell of people can catch the mosquitoes that carry malaria, for counting or for thinning their numbers. The bait here was nylon socks worn for a single day, rich in human scent.

Field tests during the malaria season compared trap designs and placements to raise the catch. A better catch gives truer counts of the local swarm and its infection rate. The tuned setup hands control teams a sharper, cheap tool that needs no power-hungry gear.
plos-pone-0008267:
Nobuo Imai and colleagues studied sustainable forestry in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Sustainable forest management was recently introduced to tropical production forests. It helps maintain timber resources over time. Whether it also helps biodiversity and carbon storage was unclear. Those extra gains are called co-benefits, and data on them were lacking.

The team estimated both benefits in managed tropical forest. Forest that stores carbon and shelters species serves two global goals at once. Evidence of co-benefits strengthens the case for sustainable practices. It can also guide payments and policies that reward careful logging.
plos-pone-0008367:
Amy L. Vincent and colleagues tested fresh pork for pandemic influenza in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The 2009 pandemic H1N1 virus emerged in humans from swine influenza lineages. That origin raised public concern over the safety of pork. Pigs infected experimentally developed respiratory disease from the virus. Whether virus persisted in meat was the key question.

The team found an absence of the pandemic virus in fresh pork. A negative result here has direct value for food safety. It reassured consumers and the pork industry during the pandemic. It also guided handling advice for infected herds.
plos-pone-0008467:
Jian Lu and co-authors survey viral hepatitis in China in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Hepatitis viruses harm the liver and burden health worldwide. Types A, B, C, and E all occur in China. Yet few reports had measured how common each type is. The team run a cross-sectional study in six regions in 2007. They test people and record infection markers.

Their data give general rates for each virus type by region. Those rates fill a gap in national health facts. Planners can use them to target vaccines and screening. The study sets a baseline for tracking change over time.
plos-pone-0008567:
Maurizio Sorice and co-authors trace a death signal in T cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. CD95, also called Fas, triggers apoptosis in immune cells. The team previously found a raft lipid called GD3 must move toward mitochondria. Its movement, linked to microtubules, was mandatory for late death events. A protein called CLIPR-59 had recently been identified as a microtubule linker. The team test if GD3 associates with CLIPR-59 during this process in lymphoblastoid T cells.

They find the GD3 and CLIPR-59 association plays a role in Fas-triggered apoptosis. The lipid and linker together help route the death signal. That association completes a path from surface receptor to mitochondria. It details how immune cells execute programmed death.
plos-pone-0008667:
Sophia Wang and co-authors study host genetics in HPV infection in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Human papillomavirus infrequently persists and progresses to cervical cancer. Most infections clear on their own. The team examined host genetic factors hypothesized to determine that subset. They test common genetic variants against HPV persistence and progression. Subjects are women infected with oncogenic HPV types. Genetic data are linked to clinical follow-up.

They find certain common variants associate with risk of persistence and progression. Host genetics thus help decide which infections become dangerous. Such variants could stratify women for closer screening. That would focus colposcopy resources on those at highest risk.
plos-pone-0008767:
Margot Bass, Matt Finer, Clinton Jenkins, and colleagues measured the global worth of Ecuador's Yasuní National Park. Their assessment appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The park protects a rich corner of the western Amazon. Beneath one remote block lie Ecuador's second largest untapped oil reserves. Drilling there would trade wildlife for revenue. Decision makers needed the park's value stated plainly.

The team tallied species richness across many groups of plants and animals. Yasuní holds record numbers for its size in the region. Those numbers make a strong scientific case for protection. The study arms conservation debates with hard counts.
plos-pone-0008867:
Masaru Yokoyama, Hiromi Mori, and Hironori Sato showed the cell's energy coin can remotely tune HIV's copying enzyme. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Reverse transcriptase converts HIV's RNA genome into DNA. It must choose the right building blocks as it copies. How it keeps that choice accurate matters for the virus's genetics. It also matters for resistance to nucleoside drugs, which mimic those blocks.

ATP, the energy molecule, bound away from the copying site yet changed selectivity. Such allosteric tuning works like a remote dial. The finding reshapes models of how the enzyme stays faithful. It may also reveal new ways to jam the copying process.
plos-pone-0008967:
Anton Stabentheiner, Helmut Kovac, and Robert Brodschneider studied how a beehive keeps its nursery warm, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Honeybee young need the brood nest held within a few degrees to grow properly. Too cold or too hot, and larvae and pupae develop badly. The colony acts like one body, warming and cooling together.

The team watched which bees do the heating and cooling work. A bee's age, its place in the hive, and the heat stress it felt all mattered. Some bees shiver to make heat; others fan or spread water to cool. The study maps how thousands of insects share one thermostat job.
plos-pone-0009067:
Khumbo Kalua and co-authors counted cases of a blinding eye infection in Malawi, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Trachoma is a neglected tropical disease caused by repeated eye infections over years. It was suspected to be endemic in Malawi, but without firm numbers. The survey covered districts in the country's centre and in the south.

Teams examined people in randomly chosen village clusters across the region. They recorded trachoma signs and the living conditions that favour spread. Crowding, water access, and sanitation all shape the risk of infection. A measured prevalence tells control programmes where surgery and antibiotics are needed most.
plos-pone-0009167:
Yonghui Zhang and co-authors compared the two surface proteins of three dangerous flu viruses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Influenza A swaps gene segments freely when two strains meet. That reassortment helps it adapt to new hosts, including humans. Hemagglutinin and neuraminidase are its two surface spikes.

The study covered a highly pathogenic bird virus and two pandemic H1N1 viruses. It charted how the spike genes match or mismatch across them. Some pairings appear linked to how nasty a strain becomes. Watching spike matching helps forecast which new viruses threaten pandemics.
plos-pone-0009267:
Koichi Hasegawa and co-authors published this worm study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Allyl isothiocyanate is the sharp compound that gives mustard and wasabi their bite. The team asked what it does to a tiny roundworm, Caenorhabditis elegans. Certain harsh chemicals switch on detox enzymes in animals, and this compound seemed to be one.

Using worms engineered as living sensors, they showed the compound raises GST and UGT enzymes. Those enzymes clear harmful products of oxidative stress. Worms treated with the compound resisted oxidative stress better. The result suggests a food chemical can prime an animal's own defenses, at least in worms.
plos-pone-0009367:
Guido Krebiehl and co-authors published this Parkinson's study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Losing the protein DJ-1 is a rare inherited cause of Parkinson's disease. DJ-1 normally helps cells handle oxidative stress and keeps mitochondria, the power plants, healthy. Mitochondrial trouble sits at the center of most theories of Parkinson's.

Cells lacking DJ-1 showed reduced baseline autophagy, the cleanup that recycles worn parts. Their mitochondria also moved and divided abnormally. The double fault leaves damaged power plants lingering instead of being cleared. That links one Parkinson's gene to a concrete failure in the cell's housekeeping.
plos-pone-0011467:
Josée Castonguay-Vanier and co-authors established in 2010 the fruit fly as a host for studying a dangerous group of bacteria. The Burkholderia cepacia complex infects the lungs of people with cystic fibrosis and can be deadly, yet studying it in mammals is slow and costly. A cheap, fast-breeding animal host would let scientists screen many bacterial variants quickly.

Fruit flies infected with the bacteria sickened in ways that tracked the bacteria's known virulence, validating the fly as a model host. With flies, researchers can test which bacterial genes matter for infection and screen candidate treatments at a pace mammal work cannot match. Findings still need confirming in mammals before clinical use. Even so, a simple model that ranks threats quickly is a practical gain for a neglected and feared infection.
plos-pone-0011567:
Uffe Nielsen and co-authors revisited in 2010 one of ecology's oldest puzzles: why a spoonful of soil holds so many animal species. The enigma is that countless tiny animals coexist in a seemingly uniform handful of dirt without the strongest simply winning. The team tested the role of small-scale heterogeneity, the patchwork of tiny habitats, pores, crumbs, and moisture gradients that fill that spoonful at the animals' own scale.

Their analysis shows that tininess itself breeds variety: at millimeter scale, soil is not one habitat but thousands, and species divide them finely. The enigma dissolves when the observer shrinks to the animals' size. The lesson travels beyond soil, to reefs, forests, and guts, wherever diversity looks impossible until the habitat is measured at the resident's scale. Conservation of soil life means protecting that fine patchwork, not just acreage.
plos-pone-0011667:
Alexander Kranjec and colleagues investigated bias in soccer refereeing, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Referees must judge fouls quickly amid fast, ambiguous contact. The authors asked whether the side of the field an incident occurs on quietly sways the decision to blow the whistle.

Their analysis found a bias linked to the left side, playing on the old meaning of sinister as left-handed. Foul calls were not evenly distributed as pure judgement would predict. The lopsided whistle shows how deep spatial biases can skew even trained officials, with lessons for any sport that relies on split-second human calls.
plos-pone-0011767:
Ruth Thurstan and Callum Roberts rebuilt two centuries of change in Scotland's Firth of Clyde, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The firth is a large sea inlet that reaches far into the west coast. The authors pulled together detailed fish catch records for the area and set them beside old written accounts to trace change driven by fishing over two hundred years.

Their record shows a long slide, which they call an ecological meltdown of this coastal system. Fish groups that once fed rich catches were reshaped beyond repair. The case warns how steady harvest with no restraint can drain even a large sea inlet.
plos-pone-0011867:
Xinping Fu and co-workers presented in 2010 a simpler way to measure how well killer T cells destroy tumor cells. Knowing that killing power matters for both basic cancer research and patient care. The long-standing standard test uses radioactive chromium released from dying target cells, which is cumbersome and hard to run often.

The new method aims for the same measurement with better sensitivity and less fuss. A practical assay lets labs compare immune treatments head to head and follow a patient's T cell strength over time. For cell therapies, where the product is living immune cells, a trustworthy killing measure is close to a quality certificate.
plos-pone-0011967:
Karine Olu and a large team mapped in 2010 the life found at cold seeps along the belt of seafloor that runs under the equator of the Atlantic. Cold seeps are spots where fluids leak from the deep seafloor and feed rich life in the dark. The work sat inside the Census of Marine Life, a world-wide effort to list what lives in the seas.

By setting the seep life of the far west side next to that of the far east, the team could see which kinds are shared. They could also see which are found in one place only. Seeps are like islands in the deep, so links between them shape how their life spreads and changes. As work in the deep sea grows, that map is base knowledge for keeping these spots safe.
plos-pone-0012067:
Elisa Cocco and co-workers showed in 2010 that a tiny RNA dials down a receptor involved in gut and immune signaling. Vasoactive intestinal peptide is a signal with immune-calming effects, and its receptor VPAC1 is known to be turned down when immune cells activate. The mechanism behind that tuning was the open question.

The team found that microRNA 525-5p negatively modulates expression of the receptor gene. A single small RNA acting as the dimmer gives the immune system a precise, reversible control. Receptor levels shape how strongly tissues answer the calming peptide, so this dial could matter in gut inflammation and other immune conditions.
plos-pone-0012167:
Sunil Sazawal, Usha Dhingra, Pratibha Dhingra, and co-authors tested nutrient-fortified milk in toddlers for PLOS ONE in 2010. Young children in poorer settings often lack several vitamins and minerals at once, and the result is anemia and stunted growth. Pills and education campaigns have had limited success, so putting the missing nutrients into a food children already drink is an appealing alternative.

In their masked, randomized trial, children on the fortified milk gained better iron status, less anemia, and better growth. A food-based fix that works at home, every day, can reach children clinics never see. Trials this size give governments solid ground for funding fortification programs.
plos-pone-0012267:
Samuel Smits and Cleber Ouverney released a web tool for drawing family trees of species, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many programs existed for printing phylogenetic trees, the branching diagrams of evolution, but the web needed trees that stay sharp at any size and respond when clicked. Their library, written in the web's standard scripting language, renders trees as crisp vector graphics inside ordinary browsers.

Interactive trees let readers zoom into a branch, search names, and rearrange the view instead of squinting at a fixed picture. For teachers, database builders, and journals moving online, that flexibility changes trees from illustrations into working tools. Software papers like this quietly raise what every later study can show.
plos-pone-0012367:
Mayu Frank, Julia Kaufman, Suyan Tian and colleagues ran an early prostate cancer vaccine trial reported in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their idea came from patients whose immune systems attacked their own tumors after nerve damage, showing that the body can mount strong anti-tumor defense. The team asked whether a vaccine could safely spark that kind of natural immunity on purpose.

The trial tested whether the vaccine was safe and whether patients' immune systems responded. The approach uses the patient's own tumor signals rather than a single lab-made target. Early trials like this one cannot prove a cure, but they show whether the concept deserves larger tests. For prostate cancer, which often grows slowly, immune treatments remain an active hope.
plos-pone-0012567:
Sharon Downes, Tracey Parker and Rod Mahon reported early resistance to a Bt toxin in an Australian cotton pest, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Bollgard II cotton makes two insect-killing Bt proteins, a pyramid meant to delay pest resistance far longer than single-toxin crops. The bollworm Helicoverpa punctigera was the species to watch, since its cousin had broken single-toxin cotton elsewhere.

Monitoring found incipient resistance to the Cry2Ab toxin — not field failure, but a measurable shift. Early warning is exactly what pyramid strategy depends on, since response is still possible. The findings press growers to keep refuge plantings and monitoring strong before resistance becomes failure.
plos-pone-0012667:
Thompson, Tipney, Brass and co-authors followed a gene switched on when mammals must make red blood cells fast. This stress response answers blood loss and anaemia, yet its molecular steps were little known. Their 2010 study names claudin 13, a member of a family of proteins that seal gaps between cells.

They show claudin 13 is controlled as part of stress-driven blood production in mice. A sealing protein playing a role in blood making is an unexpected link. It opens a new angle on how the body answers anaemia under pressure.
plos-pone-0012767:
Delaney, Riley and Fisher reported fast genetic change in four wild vertebrates squeezed by city growth. Cities chop wild habitat into fragments, and theory predicts many harms from small, cut-off populations. Their 2010 study sampled widespread species living in and around an urban area.

Despite their different lives, all four showed a strong shared genetic response to fragmentation, and it came fast. A common response hints that city living pushes evolution along set paths. The finding warns that even common species are changing genetically as cities spread.  The species ranged across birds, mammals and reptiles in scope.
pmc-11019967:
Collins, Moons, Dhiman, and co-authors publish TRIPOD+AI, updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction models. Such models estimate a patient's risk or likely outcome, and they may use plain statistics or machine learning. A first TRIPOD statement in 2015 set minimum reporting rules for these studies.

The update extends those rules for an era when learning algorithms are common in medicine. Authors are told what to report so readers can judge if a model was built and tested fairly. Clear reporting helps hospitals avoid weak models and helps good models earn trust faster.
pmc-3218867:

Thirty dogs and thirty cats took part in home based two bowl tests over four meals, choosing between a diet with ten percent microbial protein and a matched diet with ordinary protein.

Both species preferred the new diet by a clear statistical margin. Dogs ate a substantially larger share of the microbial bowl, and cats did the same on a smaller scale. Pets also approached and started on the new food first more often. Laboratory checks of the diets supported the preference readings. Pia Pennekamp and three colleagues use eye tracking to test a theory of how witnesses pick faces from a lineup, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The theory says witnesses compare features across lineup members. They lean on features the suspect does not share with the fillers, since shared features cannot distinguish anyone. The researchers digitally pasted one feature, eyes, nose, or mouth, from a target face onto every member of some lineups, then watched where one hundred participants looked.

Gaze allocation to the supposedly diagnostic features did not differ between doctored and control lineups, nor did it track whether identifications were right. Witnesses simply did not visibly weigh shared features the way the theory proposes. The authors conclude the mental comparison, if it happens, is not carried out through overt eye movements. The result trims one proposed mechanism from lineup science, leaving the accuracy question open for other explanations.

Andrés Soto published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE describing BigLoI, a system that watches Colombia's public drug-buying contracts for signs of trouble. Using open data from the national procurement platform and the drug regulator, Soto built a reproducible pipeline covering pharmaceutical contracts from 2020 to 2025. Records about veterinary or farm use were removed after human review, leaving a closed cohort of over one hundred sixty thousand contracts.

Within broad drug categories containing enough contracts, a scoring engine flagged those whose total value looked statistically unusual compared with their peers.
