Only a small fraction, well under one percent of analyzed contracts, tripped the flag, which the author presents as a watchlist for auditors rather than proof of wrongdoing. A side experiment tested smart-contract payment automation on a test network only. Soto argues that open, reproducible surveillance gives oversight bodies an early-warning tool that private audits cannot match.
plos-pone-0357767:
Qian Liu and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on malignant melanoma, the dangerous skin cancer, among East Asians aged sixty and older. Using the Global Burden of Disease 2023 dataset, they traced deaths and disability from 1990 to 2023 They then projected rates to 2040 with a multi-model forecasting system. It picked the best of seven candidate models for each place and measure.

Deaths among older adults more than doubled across the three decades, and years of healthy life lost rose steeply too, even though age-adjusted death rates barely moved. That gap points to population aging itself as the engine of the rising burden. Women showed higher incidence and prevalence, while men carried higher mortality and disability. Forecasts varied by location, with several places expected to plateau. The authors call for early-detection efforts and fair access to diagnosis and care aimed squarely at older adults.
plos-pone-0357567:
Tzu-Lan Chang and colleagues published a 2026 virology study in PLOS ONE on a workhorse of gene therapy: HIV-based lentivirus particles dressed in an envelope protein borrowed from another virus, VSV. The question was practical: how do the envelope's sugar chains change how virus particles behave in solution, and does behavior change infectivity? The team tracked particle clumping with light scattering and checked the picture with microscopy, filtration, and antibody tests.

The virus flipped between three states depending on serum, acidity, and calcium: clumped on its own, spread out, or clumped by calcium. Strikingly, the switching points sat right at the levels found in the human body, so small shifts in conditions could swing infectivity, and the three states infected cells at clearly different rates. Removing the envelope's end sugars destroyed the switching ability. Handling conditions near body-like values, they warn, can silently change a batch's potency.
plos-pone-0357667:
Tian-Qi Li and coauthors published a 2026 genetics study in PLOS ONE on tooth agenesis, the most common developmental dental disorder, in which some teeth never form. Known genes explain only part of cases. The team sequenced the protein-coding DNA of eighteen patients with the non-syndromic form. Two kinds of cluster analysis then hunted for unknown genes that keep known company.

Both clustering methods agreed, and one gene, EPB41L4A, landed in a cluster crowded with well-established tooth agenesis genes. That gene takes part in the Wnt signaling pathway, a master control system in embryonic development, which strengthens the suspicion. The authors are careful about what clustering can prove: genes grouped together tend to share functions, so EPB41L4A earns candidate status, not a verdict. It becomes a priority for follow-up experiments that could sharpen genetic counseling and diagnosis for families missing teeth.
plos-pone-0357467:
Michael O. Adu and David O. Yawson published a 2026 bibliometric study in PLOS ONE on a stark mismatch: crops feeding much of sub-Saharan Africa get little research on the organs they are harvested for. Cassava, yam, sweet potato, taro, and cocoyam supply a large calorie share, yet their root systems, which become the food, are barely studied. The authors paired food supply data from forty-six countries with nearly nine hundred publications spanning eight decades.

The region produces most of the world's cassava and nearly all yams but accounts for under a tenth of root research, clustering in Asia and North America. Potato attracts a fifth of the papers for a small calorie share; yams feed far more people for a sliver of attention, and taro and cocoyam are near-invisible. The most root-dependent countries publish almost nothing. Scenario models suggest fixing the imbalance could lift yields substantially.
plos-pone-0357367:
Netrang G. Desai and coauthors published a 2026 neuroscience paper in PLOS ONE on a structural detail braking the brain's main inhibitory receptor. GABA-A receptors, targets of sedatives, open when the messenger GABA binds, but how binding becomes opening is still murky. One amino acid, proline, sits in a linker segment of every subunit; only one subunit type carries a second proline nearby. The team inserted or removed that second proline in frog egg cells and recorded currents.

Adding the proline to the alpha subunit made the receptor far more sensitive to GABA and let channels open spontaneously with no messenger at all, as if a brake lifted. The same change in the gamma subunit did little. Removing the natural proline from the beta subunit produced mixed effects rather than simple loss. That subunit's linker proline, they conclude, acts as a molecular brake on activation.
plos-pone-0355967:
Chen Zhang and coauthors published a 2026 engineering paper in PLOS ONE on a web-based simulator. It tests the control systems of pumped storage hydropower plants before they ever run a real turbine. These plants, giant water batteries for the grid, depend on control software whose full logic is hard to validate. The platform combines physics-based plant models with a browser drag-and-drop modeling environment, so engineers assemble control logic graphically.

A governor case study showed the simulator tracking commands with tiny error. More importantly, it also exposed a dangerous overspeed weakness when a faulty actuator was injected, exactly the drills the platform exists for. Its trajectories matched an established commercial simulator almost perfectly. It ran in real time for many simultaneous sessions, and passed a hardware-in-the-loop trial. Users rated it highly. It is presented as risk-free rehearsal space that can cut commissioning failures.
plos-pone-0338067:
Michael Beraki Mengistu leads a clinical trial in Eritrea on stretching pain relief after arm surgery. Surgeons often numb the whole arm through nerves near the collarbone, but the numbness fades within hours. Sixty patients at a national referral hospital received the same nerve block, and by chance half also got a steroid drug through a vein while the rest got salt water.

Pain relief lasted more than twice as long in the steroid group, and the numbness also set in faster. Those patients asked for less extra pain medicine, and no side effects appeared in either group. Mengistu and colleagues present the cheap steroid dose as a practical upgrade for hospitals where advanced pain tools are hard to obtain.
plos-pone-0357267:
Yang Li and a team of engineers rebuild the software that checks earthquake sensor data for gaps and faults using modern cloud tools. Seismology networks now produce data faster than older server setups handle comfortably. Their design runs the quality checks in small software containers that grow or shrink with demand, guided by a scheduling method that watches processor and memory load plus task timing.

Under the same hardware budget, the cloud version answered requests about twice as fast as the older server version at both load levels tested, without changing the quality math itself. Li and colleagues are careful to limit the claim to the tested workloads. Still, the result suggests observatories can scale data checking up and down with quake activity.
plos-pone-0349467:
Jennifer Buckley and four colleagues publish a plan in 2026 for mapping research on how ready nursing students are for their internship. In Ireland and many other countries, students move from supervised classroom placements into internships where real responsibility begins, a step often marked by anxiety and shaky confidence. New Irish education standards have sharpened the focus on readiness for practice.

Following established scoping review methods, the team will search several major databases plus Irish grey literature for studies on this transition. Pairs of reviewers will screen and chart the evidence independently, looking for factors that help or hinder students as they move toward internship. The finished map should show universities and hospitals where support is strong, where it is missing, and where new research is needed.
plos-pone-0356467:
Rashedul Hoque and three colleagues explore cheaper ways to measure the electrical state of living cells, in this 2026 study. The standard tool, patch clamp, reads a single cell through a fine glass pipette; it is accurate but slow, costly, and demands rare skill. The team instead used two techniques that read thousands of cells in under a minute, one based on how cells move in an electric field and one based on light scattering.

Working with a human bladder cancer cell line, they applied three drugs known to alter cell electrical behavior and compared the cheap methods' readings with published patch clamp results. The field-based technique matched patch clamp values closely for membrane voltage and conductance. The authors argue such methods could open routine electrical testing of cells to ordinary labs and speed up drug screening.
plos-pone-0349967:
Barbara Kosińska-Selbi and seven colleagues describe a surveillance system that keeps watch over a commercial test panel for hard-to-detect respiratory bacteria, in this 2026 paper. The panel in question detects atypical pathogens such as those causing legionnaires' disease and whooping cough alongside SARS-CoV-2. Because these microbes keep mutating, a test that worked at launch can quietly lose accuracy, so regulators expect ongoing post-market checks.

The framework combines genetic sequence analysis with an artificial intelligence tool that scans new literature, flagging mutations that might affect detection. Across years of data the panel held up: coverage stayed high and cross-reactions were limited to expected ones within the whooping cough family, with a single rare, possibly critical mutation found. The authors argue such continuous, partly automated surveillance is now essential for such tests.
plos-pone-0356367:
Fayyaz Ahmad and four colleagues apply machine learning to a humble factory problem in this 2026 study: predicting how much sewing thread a garment will consume. Ordering too much thread wastes money; too little stalls production. The team focused on a common industrial stitch class. They compared six algorithms, including tree ensembles, support vector machines, and a neural network, on predicting consumption from simple inputs such as the number of fabric layers and stitch length.

An ensemble method called Extra Trees won clearly, predicting thread use with an average error of only a few centimeters and explaining the great bulk of the variation. Repeated cross-validation showed the model was stable rather than overfitted. The authors propose their prediction formula as a ready tool for garment manufacturers who want to order precisely and cut stock waste.
plos-pone-0356267:
Chloe Meewes Lewis and four colleagues search blood samples for molecular hints of who will catch chlamydia again, in this 2026 study. Reinfection is common and raises the risk of reproductive harm, yet no test predicts it. The team profiled tiny regulatory molecules called microRNAs, collected from women's blood at a treatment visit, both inside tiny released vesicles and free in serum. They then checked who tested positive again three months later.

One vesicle-carried molecule found at baseline was linked to later reinfection, while three serum molecules were linked to staying clear. The molecules' predicted targets cluster in immune T-cell pathways, with different molecules leaning toward different T-cell types. The authors stress the findings are preliminary: the candidates now need validation in larger groups before any predictive test for reinfection risk can be built.
plos-pone-0355867:
Jan Schleicher, Doreen Klingler, and Manfred Claassen release a software fix for a quiet error that can derail single-cell gene studies, in this 2026 paper. A popular technique predicts where a cell's gene activity is heading by comparing freshly made, unspliced transcripts with mature, spliced ones. Yet the field's standard counting tool was built for older sequencing chemistry. Newer protocols read from the other end of the transcript, and the old tool silently assumes the wrong direction there.

Their new command-line program, tidesurf, counts both transcript types correctly for both chemistries. On four public datasets it recovered the right counts where the old tool performed well and, crucially, where it quietly failed. The authors warn that continuing to use the legacy tool on the newer data invites wrong biological conclusions, and they position tidesurf as its up-to-date replacement.
plos-pone-0354367:
Patria Rojas and co-authors searched for social drivers of non-medical sedative and opioid use among Latino adults in the United States. Misuse is rising, and Latino-specific evidence was thin. Their 2026 analysis used a national research dataset covering more than twenty-two thousand Hispanic and Latino adults with complete records.

Recent non-medical use was rare in the sample, well under one percent for each drug class. Odds of opioid misuse rose with older age, male sex, depression, reported discrimination, and neighbourhood disorder. More schooling, higher income, being foreign-born, and speaking a language other than English at home were protective. Rojas and colleagues call for culturally fitted prevention aimed at the highest-risk subgroups.
plos-pone-0355367:
Chisho Takeoka and colleagues test in 2026 whether brain wave recordings from the scalp can sort a rare prion disease from Alzheimer's disease and healthy ageing. The prion illness, in its sporadic form, damages thinking as abnormal protein builds up in the brain, and early diagnosis is hard. Their sample was small, with only a handful of prion cases.

Measures of wave power, synchrony, and network shape fed a sorting model that reached very high accuracy in first checks and stayed well above chance in stricter tests. The authors treat the signals as promising candidates only, since larger outside samples must confirm the result before clinic use.
plos-pone-0355467:
Xing He and colleagues probe in 2026 how a low oxygen response factor affects gut inflammation and gut microbes in rats modelled with diarrhoea dominant bowel syndrome. Stressed rats developed the bowel condition, while other groups had the factor raised by thin air or lowered by a blocking drug. Colon tissue, symptoms, and stool microbes were tracked over four weeks.

Raising the factor calmed a key inflammatory pathway, while lowering it worsened symptoms and raised that pathway's signals. Microbe mixes shifted in the model, with some helpful groups falling. The authors note a link between the factor and microbes, but direct cause remains unproven.
plos-pone-0354967:
Bingjie Wang and colleagues describe in 2026 what happens to eyes where blood stains the clear front window after a severe open injury. Records came from a large eye injury study, covering a few dozen eyes that had inner eye surgery without an immediate donor cornea transplant. A washout came first, with a temporary artificial window used when the view stayed too cloudy.

Most corneas cleared at least in part on their own over time, leaving a usable edge view. Vision and eye pressure both improved by final follow up, and only one eye later needed a donor transplant. Saving the patient's own cornea is favoured.
plos-pone-0353767:
Nor Diyana Hani Ghani led a team of six authors on this 2026 study of MyKidEye, a phone app teaching parents about children's eye problems. Parents from two schools either used the app, which explains common vision problems, warning signs, and treatments, or served as a comparison group, answering knowledge, attitude, and practice surveys before and after.

Practice scores improved clearly in the app group, while knowledge and attitude gains did not reach clear significance in this short trial. Ghani presents the app as a useful support for lasting eye care habits at home.
plos-pone-0354667:
Chuanmin Zhang and four colleagues published this 2026 comparison of soccer policy in China and Japan. Using text analysis software and a policy scoring model, they examined thirty-one official football policy documents from both countries, rating the tools used, the content covered, and overall policy quality.

Both nations back development, public participation, and club building, but China leans on school football while Japan targets elite players and league strength. China's policies scored better on system design, Japan's on clear implementation and community ties. Zhang aims the lessons at improving Chinese football policy.
plos-pone-0354267:
Haitham Abu Khadija led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of a simple blood ratio that may flag risk after a heart valve procedure. More than seven hundred patients received a replacement aortic valve through a leg artery. Beforehand, the team split them by their AST to ALT ratio, two routine liver enzymes, and tracked thirty days of complications.

Patients with a high ratio faced clearly greater risks of kidney injury, stroke, and new heart rhythm problems, though not of death. Abu Khadija suggests adding this cheap marker to pre-procedure checks.
plos-pone-0352167:
Aghajan and colleagues, in a 2026 study, use systems biology to narrow the long list of genes tied to acute myeloid leukemia, a fast-moving cancer of the blood. They start from a public data set that compares gene activity in patients and healthy people. Hundreds of genes differed between the two groups.

Layer by layer, the team filtered the list: first by the jobs genes do, then by how their proteins interact, then by which genes link to patient survival. Eight genes survived the screen, three turned up and five turned down in patients. Two of the raised genes help white blood cells stick and move, while the lowered set includes genes that copy DNA. A final check looked at how these genes relate to drug response, and the picture was mixed, hinting at resistance. The authors suggest the short list could guide treatment matched to each patient's gene pattern.
plos-pone-0352967:
Homšek Ilić and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask which ready-made dosing model best predicts blood levels of infliximab, a drug used for inflammatory bowel disease. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis differ in where and how deeply the gut is inflamed, and severe forms are harder to treat. A model that fits one group may miss in another.

The team tested twenty published models against drug monitoring data from their hospital, split into five groups: all patients, severe colitis flares, Crohn's disease, fistulizing Crohn's, and ulcerative colitis. No single model passed every accuracy test. Different models led for different groups, both when predicting cold and when updated with a patient's own past readings. Some simulation checks agreed, others pointed elsewhere. The authors conclude that clinics should pick the model by disease type and severity, a step toward dosing matched to the patient rather than one average recipe.
plos-pone-0354467:
Forero and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, automate the counting of tumor cell colonies in radiation experiments. To judge whether radiation kills cancer cells, researchers grow surviving cells into colonies and count them, a slow and subjective chore by eye. Their tool, built as a plugin for a common image program, was tested on colon cancer cells.

The method finds round colonies using a shape-hunting technique, cleans the image with standard operations, and sets the smallest true colony size from a performance curve. On test images, it matched human counters closely, with sensitivity and agreement scores in the low nineties and a strong overall reliability rating. It also allows manual edits, so a researcher can fix doubtful spots. The authors say the tool can stand in for hand counting in colony survival assays, speeding a routine step in radiation biology.
plos-pone-0319367:
Lu and colleagues, in a 2026 study, build a questionnaire that asks heart failure patients how comfortable their mouths feel. Oral discomfort is common in this illness and can spoil eating, speech, and quality of life. Existing mouth checks are done by clinicians and score visible problems, missing how the patient actually feels. No patient-reported tool existed for this group.

Questions were drafted from research, patient interviews, and expert advice, then refined through two rounds of expert review. About one hundred ninety patients in three hospitals completed the final twenty-four-item questionnaire. Expert ratings of the questions were high, and the answers hung together reliably. The score related weakly to a clinician's mouth exam, just as expected for a measure of comfort. Grouping of questions supported the tool's structure. The authors present it as a first validated way to hear oral comfort in the patient's own voice.
plos-pone-0353467:
Hongliang Ma and seven co-authors compare ways of farming salty coastal land in this 2026 PLOS ONE field study from Tangshan, China. Over two years they tested three patterns against ordinary single-crop farming: rotating fresh peas with rice, raising crabs inside rice paddies, and rotating wheat with rice. They measured money earned alongside soil and chemical use.

Each pattern beat its comparison crop on income, and the rice-and-crab system earned the most. Salt in the soil eased slightly, organic matter rose, and sprays dropped by roughly a fifth to a half. The results show coastal farmers need not choose between profit and healthier soil.
plos-pone-0353267:
Barkha Yadav-Samudrala and seven colleagues give cannabidiol to aged mice carrying an HIV protein gene, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study of brain ageing with HIV. The viral protein Tat lingers in the body and harms the brain even when infection is controlled. Fifteen-to-eighteen-month-old mice, male and female, received the cannabis compound daily for twelve weeks, then faced memory and anxiety tests.

Recognition memory improved, but only in females carrying the viral gene. Pain responses shifted in all treated mice, and body temperature and weight changed without harming movement. Brain chemistry measurements showed the compound reshaped the body's own cannabis-like signalling differently by sex and region — a warning against one-size dosing.
plos-pone-0353667:
Hannah Pearl Glucksman and four colleagues put a new eye-scanning device through its paces in clinic, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The machine uses scattered laser light to measure how stiff the cornea and the eye's lens are, properties tied to diseases such as keratoconus. Thirty-three volunteers, some with that condition and some with normal vision, were scanned repeatedly on three machines by different operators.

Readings agreed closely: repeated measurements on one machine varied by only about one to two percent, and machines matched each other nearly as well. No one was harmed during testing. Consistent stiffness readings are the first requirement before such a scanner can guide eye care.
plos-pone-0352867:
Wu, Duan, and Luo studied early warning systems for online courses in a 2026 paper. Such systems flag students who may quit, but reports often skip whether the scores stay fair and trustworthy once schools act on them. The team used records from the Open University and built features from the first four weeks of study.

Nine kinds of prediction models were compared, and a tuned boosting model was kept for deeper checks. Results showed that the cutoff chosen for alerts sharply changed the balance between correct and missed warnings. Fairness also shifted with each policy choice, so the authors argue that alert rules should be set openly, not treated as fixed.
plos-pone-0351667: Brain tumor segmentation — uncertainty-aware — via Mamba-enhanced hybrid architecture. MamNet-PT is that system. The selective state-space modeling quantified doubt. The findings brought calibrated AI to neuro-oncology — segmentations that know their limits.
plos-pone-0353167:
Piersol, Colangelo, and Buckman began building a broad inventory of women's bodily experiences in a 2026 study. Older tools focus on negative feelings around monthly cycles, yet body states span good and bad feelings across many systems every day. Three hundred young women students rated how often varied body experiences occur and how pleasant each feels.

Items gathered from past research were trimmed by grouping methods, then tested for a sound structure. Early results supported a multi-part inventory rather than a single score. A fuller measure could help researchers link daily body experience with mood and health across the whole life span, not only around periods. Later work will refine and validate the tool.
plos-pone-0337867:
Stuart and colleagues interviewed family doctors championing hepatitis C care in England in a 2026 study. Many people with the infection were diagnosed years ago and lost to follow-up, while others remain undiagnosed. Fourteen doctors, most linked to regional hepatitis networks, described what helps and what blocks bringing patients back.

Doctors valued the champion role and found it rewarding. Still, system problems persisted: no payment incentives, heavy workloads, hard record searches, and weak routes for re-engaging lost patients. The authors urge joined-up work between services and care that treats the whole person. Without fixing system barriers, willing doctors alone cannot close the gap.
plos-pone-0353067:
Özkurt and Eskiler studied why elite wrestlers in Turkey plan to stay in their sport in a 2026 paper. More than three hundred seventy wrestlers answered scales on goals, basic needs, motivation, and enjoyment. Sixteen wrestlers also gave interviews about what keeps them going or pushes them away.

Enjoyment carried part of the effect of motivation onto plans to continue. Interviews added outside supports such as coaches, role models, and social backing, plus drags such as failure, unfairness, and scarce resources. Keeping elite wrestlers engaged thus depends on more than inner drive. Federations that protect enjoyment and fairness may hold talent longer.
plos-pone-0353367:
Ajmi Blout and colleagues compared childhood hardship and mental health in two Tunisian prisons in a 2026 study. One held men and one held women, with more than five hundred prisoners answering anonymous surveys on early adversity, substance use, mood, and self-worth. Women reported far more anxiety and depression than men.

Nearly half the women reported suicidal thoughts while inside, clearly more than the men. Men, in turn, more often reported low self-esteem. The authors call for rehabilitation programs that treat trauma and mental health inside prisons. Gender-specific support matters, since the heaviest burdens differed so sharply between the two prisons.
plos-pone-0334867:
Guangxing Wei, Jiayi Shen, and Xiaohan Guo present this 2026 PLOS One game-theory study of blockchain tracking in green farm supply chains. The question is who should pay to adopt it. Earlier work simply assumed the adopter in advance. Here, makers and retailers decide for themselves. The authors compare four cases: nobody adopts, retailer only, maker only, or both. They weigh two kinds of cost, set-up cost and running cost.

Whether a firm adopts eagerly, follows its partner, or refuses depends on where those costs fall. The model derives threshold values for the choice. Retailers adopting alone was the most likely outcome in the authors' case study. Very high running costs killed adoption in over half the cases studied. The thresholds give managers and officials a map for sharing the blockchain bill.
plos-pone-0352667:
Hugo Beaumont and three co-authors set out this 2026 PLOS One protocol for a scoping review. The topic is imaging in neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome. In that disputed condition, nerves are squeezed as they leave the neck and chest. It is the most common form of thoracic outlet syndrome, yet no single test confirms it. The review will map how imaging documents body variations at the junction of neck and chest, like extra cervical ribs.

As a protocol, the paper describes the plan. A three-stage search will cover databases and grey sources. Two reviewers will screen studies on their own. The team will chart which scans are used and how variations are classed. They will also chart how findings link to diagnosis and care. Studies on the blood-vessel forms are left out. The aim is to clarify imaging's role in a diagnosis built from many pieces of proof.
plos-pone-0352767:
Salim Yılmaz, Yusuf Çelik, and Elif Kara profile frailty across Türkiye's older population in this 2026 study. Frailty here spans four systems at once: movement, senses, cognition, and daily function. Their data come from a nationally representative 2023 survey. Nearly twenty-seven thousand adults aged fifty and over were included. Statistical profiling sorted people into hidden groups sharing patterns of decline across eight indicators.

Three profiles emerged. About half the older population was robust. A third sat in intermediate frailty. Roughly fifteen percent carried severe multisystem frailty. The severe group skewed heavily female: a fifth of women against under a tenth of men. Age split it too, with rates near a quarter past sixty-five. Health and lifestyle factors explained more of the pattern than money or education. For a middle-income country planning elder care, named profiles beat a single frailty score: each group needs different help.
plos-pone-0313367:
Stefanie Williams and four colleagues dissect how a community long-COVID service was built during 2020. Their 2026 mixed-methods study covers a new clinic in Hertfordshire, England. Long-COVID arrived fast, with complex symptoms and no ready-made care pathway. The service had to be reactive and responsive at once. The team mapped the journeys of one hundred sixteen patients. They also interviewed six professionals and five patients, using a behavioural framework to sort barriers from facilitators.

Patients reached the clinic on average nearly six months after falling ill. Their routes through it branched by symptoms, activating services along the way. Staff and patient accounts exposed what helped the pathway work and what blocked it. Implementation science of this kind is unglamorous and essential. Health systems keep having to stand up services mid-crisis. A documented account of one service's first five months gives the next team a head start.
plos-pone-0352267:
Franziska Trudzinski and colleagues report on a public campaign meant to make long-term breathing support on a ventilator less invisible. Few people know how many patients live with invasive ventilation at home, or what weaning from it involves. As part of the PRiVENT project, doctors, researchers, an art director, and an editor built an information campaign together.

Over about four years they posted dozens of blog pieces, hundreds of social posts, and three podcast seasons. Together these reached well over two million views, with plain-language explainers drawing the most readers. Audience makeup differed by platform, with Instagram drawing younger and more female followers. Visibility is not the same as awareness, the authors note, but the reach shows social media can carry a neglected topic far.
plos-pone-0350467:
Raffaele Ferri and colleagues lay out DREAMER, a planned Italian study of a quiet sleep finding that may warn of future brain disease. During dream sleep, muscles should go slack; in some adults they stay partly active, a sign found on sleep recordings. People with the full behavior disorder often act out dreams and later develop Parkinson-like diseases, but this milder sign, without dream acting, is poorly understood.

Four sleep centers will screen adults already having overnight sleep studies, then follow those with the isolated sign using shared rules and a standard scoring index. The cohort is built to be trial-ready, so future prevention studies can recruit quickly. No results appear in this protocol. Whether the sign proves harmless or an early risk state is exactly what the follow-up years are meant to settle.
plos-pone-0351567:
Julia Gutbrod and colleagues ran a head-to-head comparison of two bacterial enzymes that factories use to manufacture RNA, the workhorses behind messenger RNA medicines. The famous one, T7 polymerase, has been engineered for years; its cousin SP6 has been neglected, and no direct comparison existed. The team tested wild and engineered versions of both on making RNA with chemically altered letters, a trick that can improve medicines.

For long RNA products, T7 generally gave higher yields than SP6. An engineered T7 variant stood out for handling one altered letter, and the enzymes differed in how much double-stranded byproduct, an impurity that can stir the immune system, they produced. Makers of RNA therapies now have a side-by-side baseline for choosing and improving their enzyme, rather than defaulting to the familiar one.
plos-pone-0351867:
Nursing interns can come to feel cut off from their work, a state called alienation. Yang Guo and co-authors mapped how the feelings behind it connect, using answers from more than nine hundred interns at four large hospitals in Shaanxi, China, for this 2026 PLOS One study.

Rather than single causes, they built a web linking workload, moral distress, compassion fatigue, and self-judgment. A sense of personal duty and plain burnout sat at the center of the web. Stress from witnessing patient trauma formed the strongest bridge between clusters. The authors stress the map is a starting point for trials, not proof of cause.
plos-pone-0351067:
A spinal cord injury changes life for the whole family. Relatives must learn care skills quickly. Many feel unready for the task. Shuyuan Zhuang and colleagues surveyed patients and family caregivers in Hohhot, China. The survey ran between 2024 and 2025. Two hospitals took part.

Caregivers with stronger social support felt better prepared. Support also helped through a chain of effects. Backed-up caregivers carried lighter burdens. Lighter burdens meant less uncertainty about the illness. Both changes lifted readiness to give care. The authors suggest a practical step. Hospitals should strengthen family support networks, not just teach care tasks.
plos-pone-0349667:
A stiff heart that fills poorly often hides in older patients, and pacemaker wearers carry many of its risk factors. Elisabeth Santos and colleagues present a screening study plan, in PLOS One in 2026, for patients at a Portuguese hospital whose pacemakers were implanted between 2018 and 2022.

Each volunteer attends one full screening day: physical checks, a heart hormone blood test, heart tracing, detailed ultrasound, device readout, and frailty scoring. The aim is to count how many pacemaker patients quietly have this heart failure type and to describe their pacing patterns. The protocol reports design only, so prevalence results will follow.
plos-pone-0350567:
Sudden passenger surges can cascade through a subway network. A stadium crowd or a breakdown can trigger one. Nan-nan Lin and colleagues built a model to judge network resilience. Each line forms its own layer in the model. Shanghai's metro provided the test case. The study appeared in PLOS One in 2026.

Their score compares performance after a disturbance with normal performance. Crowding on platforms feeds into the score. So does the way riders split between routes. Failure spread follows percolation logic. The multilayer model held up better than simpler rivals. It kept more performance under severe attack. Repeated random trials confirmed the pattern. The results were stable, not luck.
plos-pone-0336467:
Yue Pan and colleagues studied kidney disease in a large United States cohort. Some members live with HIV. Others do not. Kidney disease is common in adults. HIV raises the risk of kidney failure. Records covered more than two thousand five hundred people. Visits ran from late 2020 into 2023.

Kidney disease appeared nearly twice as often with HIV. Mood symptoms were tested as a pathway link. Kidney harming drugs were tested the same way. Repeated visit models weighed each factor with care. Each person could appear more than once. Mood support may protect kidneys over time. Safer prescribing may help as well.
plos-pone-0351167:
Ji Hyun Yun, Jiho Park, and Hyun Kyun Ki checked whether repeating spit cultures three times helps find the germ behind pneumonia. Spit tests are standard yet often miss the culprit. Records covered one hundred and thirty two adults at a large hospital in 2021 and 2022 who gave three samples in a row, with quality and findings compared across rounds.

Sample quality and hit rates barely moved across rounds. Fungi, mostly Candida types, showed up more in later rounds, which may reflect noise more than cause. Total distinct culprits did grow by round three. High blood pressure, poor first drug choice, short gaps, and severe illness flagged who gained from repeats. Routine triple testing, the authors conclude, adds little for most patients.
plos-pone-0348567:
Amanda Bates and co-authors ran a year long trial in Australia in 2026 on home exercise for older people's arms and shoulders. Shoulder pain and weak arms limit dressing, cooking, and independence, and home programs are cheap if they truly work.

More than six hundred people aged sixty-five and over were split at random between an arm program and a leg program, each taught in three group sessions. Arm function was the main outcome, with strength, movement, and quality of life also tracked. Comparing against an active leg program, rather than nothing, gives a fair test of whether arm focused work adds real benefit.
plos-pone-0349867:
Jillian Scandiffio and co-authors published a review plan in 2026 on how toolkits that help clinicians change patient behaviour are themselves designed. Toolkits are everywhere in health care, yet nobody had mapped the theories and methods used to build them. No results are reported yet.

Following standard institute guidance, the scoping review will gather studies describing toolkit development for behaviour change support. It will chart which theories, models, and frameworks builders actually use. The gap is surprising: a field devoted to evidence based practice has little evidence about its own favourite tool. The finished map should help teams build toolkits deliberately instead of by habit.
plos-pone-0349567:
Sarah L Rossi, Amy Michals, and co-authors studied how pandemic stress affected drug and alcohol use among people living with HIV in Russia who had histories of injecting drugs. Stress and money worry surged during COVID-19, but their effect on substance use was unclear. Their 2026 analysis combined survey data from one hundred thirty-two participants in two trials with in-depth interviews.

About half reported high financial worry and a third high stress. Most reported no change in use, and among those who did, decreases outnumbered increases for opioids, cigarettes, and alcohol alike. High stress did raise the odds of reporting some change in opioid use. Interviews suggested disrupted drug access shaped patterns for some. The authors conclude pandemic pressure shifted use for a minority, mostly downward.
plos-pone-0340167:
Lalit Narayan Mishra and co-authors exposed a quiet flaw in software research: prediction models that peek at the future. Many studies claim to forecast whether a code build will pass, but some feed the model information only available after the build, inflating accuracy. Their 2026 study built a three-type taxonomy of this temporal leakage and tested it on more than one hundred seventy-five thousand builds from two platforms spanning a decade.

Removing leaky features cut one dataset's accuracy by about fifteen points, from near ninety-eight to about eighty-three percent, while a modern platform's accuracy barely moved, since its honest features suffice. Project maturity and build history predicted better than code complexity. The authors argue realistic accuracy near eighty-three percent is still deployable, and the taxonomy can audit future studies.
plos-pone-0350267:
Mauricio A Correa-Ochoa and co-authors spent a year dissecting the fine particle pollution hanging over Medellín, Colombia, a city trapped in a narrow Andean valley where dirty air pools. Their 2026 study collected more than one hundred samples at an urban background site and analyzed metals, ions, and carbon fractions to fingerprint the sources.

Daily particle levels averaged in the low twenties of micrograms per cubic meter, swinging with the seasons. Statistical analysis found five source families, led by mineral and resuspended dust and by aged secondary particles formed in the air. Local traffic and industry supplied a constant base, but the worst episodes arrived with regional wildfire smoke carried from distant river basins during dry spells. The authors call for strategies against both everyday and episodic sources.
plos-pone-0349767:
Hao Yuan, Guofang Dong, and Leilei Zhao designed a secure sharing system for medical data flowing between connected health devices, where records are sensitive and access rules are layered like hospital hierarchies. Older encryption schemes struggle with proving data origin, wasted computation, and single points of failure. Their 2026 design combines attribute-based encryption, where access follows a policy tree, with blockchain coordination among several authorities.

Shared key generation and group signatures let the authorities authenticate data sources together, with a dynamic update path for long-term safety. A stand-in re-encryption trick allows quick removal of a user's access. Security analysis claims resistance to standard attacks and collusion, and tests on a hundred-node blockchain testbed showed fast agreement and key updates. The authors argue the scheme suits real medical networks.
plos-pone-0349267:
Suoxiang Zhang and colleagues built a camera system that watches crowded pens of Hu sheep and sorts out what each animal is doing. Dense groups make this hard, since sheep block each other from view and common actions swamp rare ones in training data. The team first gathered a new image set showing thousands of sheep standing, lying, eating, and drinking on intensive farms.

Their model, KT-YOLO, reads each image at several scales at once so partly hidden animals still register, and it uses a training tweak that pays extra attention to rare actions. It beat the standard model it grew from by a clear margin and also outperformed a newer rival. The authors aim at round-the-clock welfare checks on busy farms without extra staff.
plos-pone-0349167:
Madeleine Ennis and colleagues interviewed twenty-eight Canadian health workers about what helps and hinders care when a pregnancy is ended in the second or third trimester for medical reasons. The group included fetal medicine specialists, genetic counsellors, nurses, and social workers from all ten academic centres offering this care. Conversations ran in English or French and were analysed for shared themes.

Six themes emerged, led by committed staff who nonetheless face burnout and discomfort around abortion care. A dedicated coordinator, workable team structures, and guidelines that balance fairness with flexibility all shaped how care felt. Workers also stressed adjusting care to each patient's lived situation. The authors map these factors so services can be organised more compassionately and evenly.
plos-pone-0348367:
Yanyan Fan and co-authors set out a protocol for mapping what is known about getting heart failure patients involved in planning their own discharge from hospital. Poor discharge planning sends many of these patients back to hospital within weeks. Their scoping review will sweep twenty databases for studies of any design that describe ways to draw adult patients into discharge decisions, then chart the strategies and the outcomes each study reported.

Two reviewers will screen and extract the evidence independently, and an established framework will organise the findings into patterns, advances, and gaps. No results are included, since the review has not yet been run. The authors expect the map to show clinicians and policymakers which involvement strategies have real support and where practice runs ahead of proof.
plos-pone-0347767:
Andy Domínguez-Monterroza, Antonio Jiménez-Martín, and Alfonso Mateos Caballero look at world stock markets as one linked network. Their 2026 paper blends three math lenses: one for shared market swings, one for local weak points in the web of links, and one for the shape of the whole structure. Daily index data over six recent years feed the analysis.

Clear shifts in market structure showed up during the COVID-19 pandemic. Another reshaping appeared in early twenty twenty-two, around the start of the war in Ukraine. Each lens caught a different side of the stress, from crowd-like swings to local fragility. Together they offer watchdogs a richer way to spot when the global system grows brittle.
plos-pone-0349067:
Seung-Bo Park and co-workers test whether simply tasting carbohydrate, without swallowing it, sharpens hard cycling. Rinsing the mouth with a sweet drink is thought to wake up the brain and ease effort. Their 2026 trial has eleven trained cyclists ride a short time trial under three setups: a carbohydrate rinse, music, or a plain rinse, with brain oxygen tracked by head sensors.

The carbohydrate rinse raised oxygen in a front brain area tied to focus. Riders also felt the work was easier, finished faster, and held higher power than under the other setups. Thinking test scores after the ride were better too. A rinse that never reaches the stomach still changed both brain and performance.
plos-pone-0347867:
Usman Rafi and co-workers build a lean computer model that spots several eye diseases from photos of the back of the eye. Full-size models need heavy computing, which many clinics lack. Their 2026 paper trims a mobile-friendly network and pulls useful detail from its middle layers, keeping the file small and the running cost low.

On a public set of retinal photos, the slim model beat a dozen larger rivals on accuracy. It also judged each image in a few thousandths of a second. A second outside dataset confirmed it still worked well beyond its training photos. Fast, light tools like this could bring eye screening to clinics with modest computers.
plos-pone-0348867:
Worrawit Wanitsuwan and co-workers use whole-genome reading to find families in southern Thailand carrying Lynch syndrome, an inherited flaw in DNA repair that sharply raises colon cancer risk. Their 2026 study sequences patients with colon or related cancers who met clinical warning signs for the syndrome.

About one in five patients carried a suspect change in a repair gene. One change appeared in ten patients who turned out to share common ancestry. Testing their relatives found fifteen more carriers, and scope checks caught growths in some before cancer formed. The math favored genetic testing over scoping every relative blindly, and the work shows how one family's testing can protect dozens of kin.
plos-pone-0348067:
Hakan Kuru explores why employees almost never use the mental health support their workplace offers. Fewer than five in a hundred typically sign up, even when help is free and private. The 2026 study interviews thirteen workers at a Turkish high-tech firm who had never used the service, then invites staff to redesign it together.

Non-use grew from several tangled causes, not one big barrier. Workers were unsure the service fit their problems, daily routines left no easy opening, and pride in a tough professional image clashed with asking for help. Together they proposed simpler entry points, support woven into normal workflows, and visible backing from leadership. The case shows access alone does not equal use.
plos-pone-0338867:
Yixi Xu and co-workers audit the photo collections used to train artificial intelligence that diagnoses middle ear infections from eardrum images. Biased training photos can make a smart tool fail in new clinics. Their 2026 study probes three public datasets from Chile, the United States, and Türkiye, covering parts of images and shifting colors to see what the models truly rely on.

Two datasets carried heavy bias: models scored high at home yet leaned on irrelevant marks and flopped abroad. A model trained on meaningless features from one set still scored well on the other biased set, proving the flaw. The third set leaned more on real clinical features. Standard photo rules and wider sampling are needed before such tools earn trust.
plos-pone-0346967:
Jean-Philippe Kröll and colleagues compared two ways of scanning the brain: letting people rest quietly in the scanner, and letting them watch films instead. Their 2026 paper asks whether measures of brain networks give the same answer when the scan is repeated, a basic requirement if such measures are ever to guide medical care.

Watching films made the network measures more consistent from one session to the next than resting did. The gain, however, depended on which film was shown and which network was measured. It also differed between the group's Asian and European participants. The authors encourage film viewing in future studies, while warning that the choice of film needs care.
plos-pone-0348267:
Ke Wang, Yong Zhou, Jingchi Yan, and Yuejie Zhang reconstructed how rivers once carried sediment into a sinking fault basin in northeast China's Songliao region during the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods. Understanding these source-to-sink routes helps explorers find oil and gas reservoirs. Using seismic surveys, drill cores, and well logs, the 2026 study divided the basin fill into six layered units.

A major fault proved most active in its middle stretch and peaked late in the intense rifting phase. Early on, steep fans spilled from the basin edges; later, long axial river systems delivered braided deltas as the broken landscape merged into one broad lake. The maps give exploration teams a clearer template.
plos-pone-0347567:
Norifumi Fujii, Katsuki Takahashi, Raki Kawama, and Taku Wakahara tested a popular coaching belief: that stiffer calf muscles make sprinters faster. Earlier reports linked stiffness of the medial gastrocnemius, the big calf muscle, to better race times. The team measured stiffness with ultrasound shear waves in twenty-one male college sprinters, at rest and during contractions, then filmed their top-speed running.

Stiffness, however measured, failed to correlate with race time or with any stride ingredient: step length, step frequency, flight time, or ground contact. The authors conclude calf stiffness may simply not matter for how sprinters move at this performance level, whatever its role elsewhere in the body.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Adopted in 1999, Resolution 1267 answered a refusal by the Taliban in Afghanistan. The Taliban would not hand over Usama bin Laden. The United States had indicted him for the 1998 bombings of its embassies in Kenya and Tanzania. The Council ruled that sheltering terrorists threatened world peace. It acted under Chapter VII, the Charter chapter that allows binding sanctions.

The text orders the Taliban to shut down terrorist training camps. It also demands that bin Laden be surrendered for trial. If the Taliban refused, all countries would freeze Taliban funds. Taliban-linked aircraft would be barred from landing or taking off, starting 14 November 1999. A new committee of all Council members would name the targeted funds and planes and police the bans.

One day before the September 11 attacks, the Council quietly closed a chapter on Kosovo. Resolution 1367 was adopted unanimously on 10 September 2001. It dealt with the arms embargo placed on Yugoslavia in 1998. That ban had been part of the pressure over Kosovo.

Members noted that the conditions for lifting the ban were now met. They therefore ended the embargo outright. They also dissolved the committee that had policed it. The text still voices worry about security along Kosovo's boundary. It backs the authority of UN officials and the NATO-led force to control weapons moving in and out of Kosovo.

Jerusalem's status drew the Council's sharpest words in 1969. Israel had held the east of the city since 1967. Fresh steps there seemed to change its face. Past UN texts had banned such moves. Resolution 267 passed with no dissent on 3 July 1969. Both sides had been heard.

The Council stood by its 1968 text on the city. It voiced deep regret that Israel had shown no heed to past calls. It blamed, in the strongest terms, all steps to change the city's status. Laws and acts that claimed to do so were judged void. Land seized in the city could not change its fate. Israel had to scrap such steps at once. It had to tell the Council its plans with no more delay.

Mauritania's seat was won the same day as Mongolia's. The two bids formed a pair deal in 1961. The West African land had left French rule the past fall. Its bid named it an Islamic republic. One state voted no, and one more held back. Resolution 167 passed on 25 October 1961 at the same meet as its twin text.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Mauritania. The Assembly did so two days hence. The deal that freed both bids was a Cold War swap. East and West each let one blocked name through. Nouakchott's flag joined the hall's rows that week. Sand, iron, and a small host of folk made up the new state. Its seat has held through coups and wars since, a mark of how wide the UN's door swung in those years.

Resolution 1667, adopted on 31 March 2006, extends the UN mission in Liberia into the autumn. Liberia had just inaugurated President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf and installed an elected government after years of war and transitional rule. Big problems remained: former fighters still needed jobs and reintegration, and the security sector was being rebuilt from scratch.

The Council extended UNMIL's mandate until 30 September 2006, and kept in place the arrangement letting its troops reinforce the sister mission in Côte d'Ivoire. It also welcomed a striking development days earlier: former president Charles Taylor, long sheltered in Nigeria, had been handed over to Sierra Leone's Special Court to face trial.

Small arms and hired guns in West Africa are the twin threats in Resolution 1467. It passed by a full vote on 18 March 2003. The text adopts a short statement on both problems. Cheap guns and paid fighters, it says, stir up wars in the region. They also feed grave abuses of rights and of the laws of war.

States in the region were asked to make sure their plans to curb these threats are put to work. They should join hands to find the men and groups who trade in guns or back hired fighters. Town groups and civic bodies should help enforce the regional ban on small arms sales. The aim was less talk, more action.

Timor-Leste steadies in Resolution 1867, adopted on 26 February 2009. The country had recovered from the 2006 crisis and the February 2008 attacks, a weapons collection had ended, displaced people had gone home, and the 'petitioners' group had disbanded. Poverty was rising, and the situation, though calm, stayed fragile. National police were preparing to resume policing duties district by district.

The Council extends the UN Integrated Mission in Timor-Leste, UNMIT, until 26 February 2010 at current strength. It supports the phased handover of policing to the national police, the PNTL, starting in 2009 wherever agreed readiness criteria are met, with UNMIT police keeping public security in the meantime. It asks UNMIT to support the 2009 local elections and keep training and mentoring the PNTL. It stresses security-sector reform, clear lines between the army and police, and action on the 2006 inquiry's recommendations. A report is due by 30 September 2009.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 48/267 was adopted on 19 September 1994. It set up the Mission for the Verification of Human Rights and of Compliance with the Commitments of the Comprehensive Agreement on Human Rights in Guatemala. Talks between the Government of Guatemala and the Unidad Revolucionaria Nacional Guatemalteca had restarted that January. They produced a framework deal, a full human rights agreement, and accords on resettlement and on a truth body.

The mission was created for a first term of six months. It was to check that the human rights promises were kept, even before a final peace was signed. Both parties were called on to back the mission fully, above all on its members' safety. They were called on to press on toward a firm and lasting peace.

Resolution 69/67 covers how the Chemical Weapons Convention is carried out. The General Assembly adopted it at its sixty-ninth session in 2014. It records that all of Syria's declared chemical weapons material and equipment had been removed by 23 June 2014. Destruction of that material abroad was still to be done. So were destruction of twelve remaining production facilities, and completion of inspections. It also backs the OPCW fact-finding mission on alleged chlorine use. It notes that Libya, Russia and the United States had missed the final extended destruction deadline of 29 April 2012.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Candidates for permanent judge posts at the Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal are forwarded on 14 October 2004. As with earlier elections, the Council's role is to pass the nominations received by the Secretary-General to the General Assembly, which elects the judges. The tribunal was by then working under a completion strategy to finish its trials.

The forwarded list names twenty candidates from countries across Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Americas. Several had already served on the tribunal. The General Assembly would choose the permanent judges from this list. Those elected would staff the trial and appeals chambers as the tribunal heard its remaining war crimes cases from the Balkan wars of the 1990s.

Serious violations of the Temporary Security Zone continued when UNMEE, the Ethiopia-Eritrea mission, was extended for six months on 30 July 2007. Deep concern is voiced. The Algiers Agreements and the Boundary Commission's ruling still waited to be carried out on the ground.

The parties are called on to keep their full commitment to the ceasefire agreement and to the zone's integrity. Ethiopia is called on to reduce the extra forces it had moved near the zone. Both parties are told to give UNMEE full access, help, and protection, and member states are asked to keep funding the trust fund that supports the demarcation process.

The arms embargo on the Democratic Republic of the Congo was adjusted on 20 December 2022, when the Council adopted Resolution 2667. The Council said the situation in the country remained a threat to international peace and security in the region. The embargo had first been set out in Resolution 1807 of 2008.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council confirmed that the embargo still covered all non-governmental groups and individuals operating in Congo. At the same time, it lifted the advance notice duties that had applied to arms shipments. That change eased the rules for Congo's government. Congo was asked to send a confidential report by 31 May 2023. The report had to explain how the country manages, stores, marks, and guards its weapons stockpiles.

Part of Cyprus was declared a separate Turkish state in February 1975, and the Republic of Cyprus complained to the Council. The one-sided declaration of 13 February deepened the island's crisis. There had been no progress in carrying out earlier decisions. Resolution 367 was adopted without a vote on 12 March 1975.

The Council called on all states to respect Cyprus's sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity. Cyprus was also to stay non-aligned. The Council regretted the February decision. It said the step tended to harm the talks between the two communities. The decision did not settle Cyprus's final political future in advance. The Secretary-General was asked to open a fresh mission of good offices. Both communities were told to give the new talks high priority.

Diplomats in occupied Kuwait lost their legal protection in 1990, when Iraq ordered the embassies there to close. Iraqi forces raided embassy grounds and seized people who held diplomatic protection. Iraq was a party to the Vienna Conventions on diplomatic and consular relations, which set the rules it was breaking. Resolution 667 followed that year.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council strongly condemned Iraq's actions. The attacks on embassy grounds and staff were condemned, including the seizures of foreign nationals. Iraq had to release the people it had seized at once. Everyone covered by Resolution 664 was included in that demand. Iraq also had to protect diplomats and missions in both Kuwait and Iraq. It had to obey the Vienna Conventions and the Council's resolutions in full. The Council decided to consult urgently on further concrete measures.

The Netherlands renewed its military action in Indonesia in December 1948, and the Council's December orders were not fully carried out. Dutch forces still held parts of the Republic's land. A good offices committee had reported on the situation, and the Council approved its reports. Resolution 67 was adopted on 28 January 1949.

The Council called on the Netherlands to stop all fighting at once. The Republic was called on to order its fighters to end their attacks. The Dutch had to free all prisoners taken since 17 December 1948. Officials of the Republic had to be let back to Jogjakarta. The text also urged quick talks. Their goals were a caretaker government, free elections, and a free United States of Indonesia. Full rule was to pass from the Netherlands by 1 January 1950, if possible.
un-sc-res-1267:
The Taliban's sheltering of terrorists brought sanctions in the autumn of 1999. On 15 October 1999 the Security Council demanded that the Taliban hand over Usama bin Laden. He had been indicted for embassy bombings in Africa. The Council also told the Taliban to stop giving shelter and training to terrorists. It recalled earlier unmet demands on the same points. Afghanistan's suffering under factional rule ran through the text.

If the Taliban failed to comply, sanctions would start on 14 November 1999. Afghan aircraft linked to the Taliban would be grounded abroad. Taliban funds and property overseas would be frozen. A committee would police the measures. The regime stalled, and the sanctions took effect on schedule.
un-sc-res-267:
Jerusalem's status returned to the Council in the summer of 1969. Israel had taken more steps to change the city's standing since 1968. On 3 July 1969 the Council restated its resolution 252 in full. It deplored Israel's failure to respect the earlier United Nations decisions. Land gained by conquest, it repeated, cannot be kept. Jordan and Israel had both addressed the members.

Israel had to tell the Council without delay what it meant to do. If the answer was negative, or if none came, the Council would meet again. It would then weigh further steps to give its decisions effect. The warning gave the text a harder edge than a simple restatement. Jerusalem's status remains contested to this day.
un-sc-res-1667:
Liberia's United Nations mission was extended on 31 March 2006, as a newly elected government took office. The Council welcomed the inauguration of President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf and the installation of her government. It also welcomed the transfer of former president Charles Taylor to the custody of the Special Court for Sierra Leone. Big tasks remained in reintegrating former fighters and rebuilding the security sector.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the United Nations Mission in Liberia, UNMIL, to 30 September 2006. Provisions allowing troops to shift between UNMIL and the Côte d'Ivoire operation ran for the same period. The Council restated its intent to authorize such temporary redeployments as needed. It noted the Secretary-General's letter of 22 March 2006 on the Côte d'Ivoire mission's tasks and troop levels. It also asked him to review his drawdown advice for UNMIL in light of Liberia's improving stability.
un-sc-res-1467:
Small arms and mercenaries in West Africa were the subject of a Security Council declaration adopted on 18 March 2003. The Council attached a full declaration to the short resolution. It voiced profound concern at how the spread of small arms and light weapons, and the use of mercenaries, harmed peace and security in the region.

The declaration asks the states of the subregion to put into effect the measures they had adopted at national, regional, and global levels. It urges them to strengthen cooperation so traffickers and mercenary backers can be identified. National commissions and civil society should be drawn into applying the ECOWAS moratorium on small arms of October 1998 and the 2001 United Nations programme of action. Wider steps are listed, from sharing data on arms buys to tighter transfer controls.
un-sc-res-1867:
Timor-Leste came under formal Council review in Resolution 1867, adopted on 26 February 2009. Calm had returned after the 2006 crisis and the attacks of February 2008. A six-week drive had collected and destroyed weapons across the country. Many displaced people had gone home, yet poverty was rising.

The text extends the United Nations Integrated Mission in Timor-Leste, called UNMIT, until 26 February 2010. National police should take back policing duties step by step during 2009, once they meet agreed standards. The mission will back local elections planned for 2009. It must also keep training police and judges, and help the government fight poverty and create jobs.
un-sc-res-1367: On 10 September 2001, Resolution 1367 on Yugoslavia was adopted unanimously. An arms embargo had been imposed in 1998 during the Kosovo crisis. The Council finds that every condition it set for lifting the ban has now been met. Acting under Chapter VII, it ends the embargo at once. The committee that watched over the ban is dissolved. The text notes the tense border near Kosovo. Arms flows there stay under the control of the peace force and the UN envoy.
europmc-pmc10044767:
Maldonado and co-authors review the hallmarks of aging and the role of oxidative stress in a 2023 paper. Aging brings a slow decline in body function and a higher risk of diseases such as cancer, heart disease, and dementia. Scientists describe that decline through a set of shared hallmarks, or marks, seen across species.

The review focuses on oxidative stress, the damage done when oxygen-based waste overwhelms cell defenses. It links that stress to each hallmark of aging. The paper helps readers see aging as a set of processes that science can study and perhaps slow.
europmc-pmc10160267:
Kocak and co-authors present CLEAR, a step-by-step reporting checklist for radiomics research, in a 2023 paper. Radiomics extracts large sets of numbers from medical scans and uses them to guide care decisions. The field holds real promise, yet most studies stay in academia because methods and reporting vary too much to trust.

The checklist walks authors and reviewers through each stage of a radiomics study. Two major European societies endorse the text. Clearer reporting should help separate strong studies from weak ones and move the best methods toward patient care.
europmc-pmc10232367:
Lorach and a large team report that a brain-spine interface let a man with spinal cord injury walk naturally again, in a 2023 study. A spinal injury cuts the line between the brain and the cord regions that drive walking, which causes paralysis. The team built a digital bridge to restore that lost link.

Sensors on the brain read the man's intent to move, and a stimulator on the cord turned those signals into leg movements. He could walk with crutches and handle varied ground. The work marks a step toward restoring movement after paralysis.
europmc-pmc10287567:
Sikkema and a huge consortium present an integrated cell atlas of the human lung in health and disease, in a 2023 study. Single-cell methods can profile each cell in a tissue, but single studies cover few donors and often disagree on cell type names. Merging many datasets can fix both problems at once.

The team combined lung datasets into one atlas spanning millions of cells. They aligned cell types across studies and mapped rare and diseased states. The atlas gives researchers a shared reference for lung biology, asthma, fibrosis, and infection research.
europmc-pmc10372067:
Garrido-Trigo and colleagues mapped immune cells in the inflamed gut at fine scale. Two long-term gut diseases drive that swelling: ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. Patients differ widely in signs and in response to drugs, for reasons still unclear. The team read gene activity in single cells from human gut tissue.

The biggest gaps between patients sat in one cell branch, the myeloid cells. That branch holds macrophages and neutrophils, two types of white blood cell. A spatial scan then placed each subtype in the tissue. Place alone split macrophages into still more kinds. Garrido-Trigo also found a strong signal web between macrophages and inflamed support cells. The work points drug research toward those two cell groups.
europmc-pmc10384267:
Obidiro, Battogtokh, and Akala reviewed care options in 2023 for a hard form of breast cancer. The form is called triple negative, since its cells lack three known drug targets. Those targets are two hormone sensors and the HER2 protein. Survival rates for this form lag behind other breast cancers.

Chemo drugs stay the most used treatment, often before or after surgery. Obidiro also covers immune therapy, targeted drugs, and beam therapy. Two flaws limit chemo: cancer cells learn to resist it, and it harms healthy cells too. The review points to tiny drug carriers, called nanoparticles, as a way past both flaws. Trials of such carriers form part of the future outlook.
europmc-pmc10546867:
The GBD 2021 Rheumatoid Arthritis Collaborators tracked the burden of rheumatoid arthritis from 1990 to 2020. The disease is a chronic immune fault that attacks the joints. It brings pain, disability, and early death. The study spans 204 nations and areas, with forecasts to 2050.

In 2020, an estimated 17.6 million people lived with the disease. Rates per head had risen 14.1% since 1990. Women carried the disease at 2.45 times the rate of men. Deaths fell over the span, to 38,300 in 2020. Years lived with disability made up 76.4% of the total health loss. The team forecasts 31.7 million cases by 2050. Smoking was the one risk factor counted.
europmc-pmc10570367:
Verkhratsky and co-authors cast astrocytes as a new frontier for brain therapy in 2023. Astrocytes, also called astroglia, are support cells that keep the brain and spinal cord stable. They guard nerve tissue and join in its defence. In each brain disease, their acts can help or harm the outcome.

The review sorts their disease states into four kinds. Verkhratsky names swollen reactive states, worn states with lost function, cell death, and rogue forms that drive disease. States shift with the illness, its stage, age, and sex. The team walks through trauma, stroke, infection, epilepsy, and decline diseases. Each state may yield its own drug strategy, they argue.
europmc-pmc11019967:
Collins and a large team present updated reporting rules for medical prediction models in this 2024 statement. Prediction models estimate a patient's risk or diagnosis and guide care choices. The older TRIPOD rules from 2015 set the minimum for reporting such studies. Since then, AI methods have spread through model building, so an update was needed.

The new TRIPOD+AI checklist holds 27 items and replaces the 2015 list, which the authors say should no longer be used. It applies whether a model was built with classic regression or with machine learning. A shorter companion checklist covers study summaries. Each item comes with fuller explanation than before. The team states the goal plainly: complete and open reporting so readers can appraise a model and judge whether to use it.
europmc-pmc1141267:
Förstemann and colleagues identify a partner protein required to mature small gene-silencing RNAs in fruit flies in this 2005 study. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs, 21 to 23 letters long, that control target genes. They are cut to size in two steps by enzymes called Drosha and Dicer. The team tested a double-stranded RNA-binding protein called Loquacious, a relative of a human protein.

Loquacious proved necessary for Dicer-1 to process precursor microRNAs normally, they found. Silencing of a reporter gene and of an endogenous gene locus both failed without it. In mutant ovaries, germ-line stem cells were not maintained properly. The protein binds Dicer-1 directly, forming a working pair. The authors note every known Dicer-family enzyme in the fly is paired with such a binding partner. The finding completes the maturation pathway picture.
europmc-pmc11829167:
Major Depressive Disorder Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium led a huge 2025 study of depression genes. The team combined data from 29 countries. Their sample held about 689,000 people with major depression. A control group held more than 4.3 million people without it.

Across the genome, the team found 697 links at 635 places. Nearly 300 of those places were new. Many links point to brain cells and to drug targets now in use. Scores built from the data predicted depression risk across ancestries. The findings open new paths for treatment research. Fine mapping also pinned down 308 genes with high confidence for follow-up work.
europmc-pmc11836267:
Liu and co-authors reviewed energy use in the body in 2025. Cells burn fuel through paths that free stored energy. Key paths break down sugar, fats, and amino acids. Others build energy carriers inside cell power stations called mitochondria.

When balance fails, disease often follows. The review links faulty energy use to cancer, brain disease, and immune disorders. Three master switches get close attention for their control roles. Liu also surveys new tools, from glowing probes to tiny materials. Those tools may turn energy science into new treatments. It appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy.
europmc-pmc1253667:
Hauser and co-authors tracked urine phthalate levels in men over three months in 2004. Eleven men gave up to nine urine samples each. Eight breakdown products were measured with precise lab methods. The goal was judging whether one sample can represent average exposure.

Five products appeared often across samples. Monoethyl phthalate showed in every single sample. Four others appeared in over 90 percent of samples. Levels swung a lot within the same man over time. Hauser quantifies how much a single sample can misclassify exposure. That matters for any study tying phthalates to health.
europmc-pmc1282567:
Sommer made the case for immune gene diversity in wildlife studies in 2005. Conservation genetics usually tracks neutral DNA markers. Those markers miss adaptive change, the kind that affects survival. The major histocompatibility complex, or MHC, is her prime example.

MHC variants shape immune recognition and disease susceptibility. They also affect odors, mate choice, kin recognition, and pregnancy. Pathogen pressure likely maintains MHC variety over time. Two mechanisms dominate: advantage of mixed copies and rarity advantage. Sommer argues coding genes like MHC must enter conservation planning. It appeared in Frontiers in Zoology in 2005.
europmc-pmc1332667:
Wasserman and colleagues tested manganese in drinking water and child intellect in 2006. Inhaled manganese is a known adult nerve toxin. Drinking water effects were nearly unstudied. The study covered 142 ten-year-olds in Araihazar, Bangladesh.

Their tube wells averaged 793 micrograms of manganese per liter. Arsenic in the same water averaged only 3 micrograms per liter. Children took adapted Wechsler intelligence tests at a field clinic. Scores were adjusted for social and social factors. Wasserman isolates manganese effects in a setting famous for arsenic. Blood tests checked lead and manganese in each child.
europmc-pmc1560167:
Health budgets force hard choices among treatments. Baltussen and Niessen argued in 2006 that those choices weigh many criteria at once: total health gain, fairness for the worst off, and urgent need. Policymakers often decide by gut feel or politics, dropping key facts.

Single-criterion tools each cover one slice, like cost-effectiveness or disease burden. The pair propose multi-criteria decision analysis, a method long used in other fields. It lays all criteria out in the open and weighs them together. Baltussen calls it a route to rational, transparent priority setting in health care.
europmc-pmc1847467: Structural and functional analysis of cellular networks with CellNetAnalyzer. — a 2005 science paper on the CellNetAnalyzer net tool. It analyzes the cellular networks. The paper is the CellNetAnalyzer guide: the findings on the net tool, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1874167: Predicted exposures to steroid estrogens in U.K. rivers correlate with widespread sexual disruption in wild fish populations. — a 2005 science paper on hormones in rivers. It links the estrogens to fish ills. The paper is the hormone-river study: the findings on fish disruption, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1880867: Oxidative stress and diabetic retinopathy. — a 2005 science paper on oxidative stress and eye ills. It reviews the stress link. The paper is the stress review: the findings on diabetic eyes, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc1924867: CRISPR recognition tool (CRT): a tool for automatic detection of clustered regularly interspaced palindromic repeats. — a 2005 science paper on the CRT CRISPR finder. It detects the CRISPR repeats. The paper is the CRT guide: the findings on the CRISPR tool, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2100367: Measuring the burden of neglected tropical diseases: the global burden of disease framework. — a 2005 science paper on measuring tropical-disease burden. It measures the disease burden. The paper is the burden study: the findings on tropical ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2362067: A genome-wide association study identifies protein quantitative trait loci (pQTLs). — a 2008 science paper on protein gene hunts. It identifies the pQTLs. The paper is the pQTL study: the findings on protein ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2386967: A low dose of dietary resveratrol partially mimics caloric restriction and retards aging parame — a 2008 science paper on resveratrol mimicking dieting. It partially mimics the restriction. The paper is the mimic study: the findings on aging ills, filed here in session.
