europmc-pmc2538567: Tracing the source of campylobacteriosis. — a 2008 science paper on finding the campy germ's source. It traces the germ source for labs. The paper is the trace study: the findings on germ ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2586367: COPI complex is a regulator of lipid homeostasis. — a 2008 science paper on COPI lipid regulation. It regulates the lipid homeostasis. The paper is the COPI study: the findings on lipid ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2627667: Zoonotic tuberculosis due to Mycobacterium bovis in developing countries. — a 2008 science paper on zoonotic TB. It studies the zoonotic tuberculosis. The paper is the TB study: the findings on bovis ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2631467: Depression and body mass index, a u-shaped association. — a 2008 science paper on depression and body mass. It finds the u-shaped association. The paper is the association study: the findings on depression, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2683567: Regulation of mammary stem/progenitor cells by PTEN/Akt/beta-catenin signaling. — a 2008 science paper on mammary stem regulation. It regulates the stem cells. The paper is the regulation study: the findings on mammary ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2695767: Epigenetic Regulation of HIV-1 Latency by Cytosine Methylation — a 2008 science paper on HIV sleep-switch marks. It reads the sleep-switch marks for labs. The paper is the mark study: the notes on HIV ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2696767: Prostate cancer-derived urine exosomes: a novel approach to biomarkers for prostate cancer. — a 2008 science paper on urine exosomes. It finds the prostate biomarkers. The paper is the biomarker study: the findings on prostate ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2700967: The natural statistics of audiovisual speech. — a 2008 science paper on sight-and-sound talk. It studies the talk stats for labs. The paper is the talk study: the findings on talk ills, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc2714467: A parsimony approach to biological pathway reconstruction/inference for genomes and metagenomes — a 2008 science paper on simplest-path gene maps. It draws the gene maps for labs. The paper is the map study: the notes on gene ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2784367: Intensive care adult patients with severe respiratory failure caused by Influenza A (H1N1)v in — a 2008 science paper on H1N1 ICU patients. It studies the severe respiratory failure. The paper is the failure study: the findings on influenza ills, filed here in session.
crantz-history-greenland-1767:
David Crantz, a Moravian missionary historian, published The History of Greenland in English in 1767. The work runs to two volumes. Crantz drew on the records of the Moravian mission, whose brethren had lived among Greenland's Inuit people for decades.

Whales, icebergs, and northern lights fill his natural history. He describes Inuit hunting, dress, and belief in close detail for European readers. Mission history runs through the whole, earnest and detailed. Sea monster lore lingers at the edges of his sober pages. The book gives the Arctic world as missionary eyes saw it in full, ice, people, and marvels together.
plos-pone-0004967:
Metabolism is a web of thousands of chemical reactions. Modelers know the exact speed of only a few of them. Osbaldo Resendis-Antonio tackled that gap in PLOS ONE in 2009. He proposed dynamic modeling for networks where kinetic information is lacking. The aim is a fuller grasp of how phenotype follows from dynamics.

High-throughput data now describe metabolism in bulk. Models struggle to use that data without rate constants. The method fills the missing speeds in a principled way. Researchers can then simulate how the whole network responds. The approach bridges a stubborn data gap in systems biology.
plos-pone-0005067:
The CDKN2A gene makes two tumor suppressors, INK4a and ARF. They force damaged cells into senescence, a permanent retirement. Jeffrey Irelan and colleagues screened for new switches on INK4a. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The screen was genome-scale, using cDNA overexpression. A reporter gene marked INK4a activity.

The screen revealed MEOX2 as a transcriptional activator of INK4a. A new player joins the cell's anti-tumor alarm system. The finding fills a gap in the cancer-defense network. Activators of tumor suppressors are valuable. Turning them up could help cells retire before they turn malignant. The study also proves the screening strategy. It can find regulators that targeted guesses would miss.
plos-pone-0005167:
A mother rat's licking and grooming shapes her pups' brains. The effects on the hippocampus were well known. Laura Smit-Rigter and colleagues looked at another region in PLOS ONE in 2009. They examined cortical layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons. These are key cells of the thinking cortex. Variations in maternal care were their variable.

Differences in care changed the neurons' dendritic structure. Their function changed along with their branching. The effects lasted into the offspring's adult life. Early care writes lasting wiring beyond the hippocampus. The work extends the mother's touch to the cortex. It deepens the biology of early-life influence. Such findings inform how early environments shape adult brains.
plos-pone-0005267:
Cells attach small tags called SUMO to proteins to change what those proteins do. Tagging helps cells handle transcription, repair DNA, and answer damage. Chen and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 that yeast tags its largest transcription protein after ultraviolet light.

The protein, Rpb1, is the core of the machine that reads genes into RNA. It received SUMO tags after UV radiation and also when transcription was impaired. The tag looks like part of the cell's alarm response, marking the reading machine when DNA trouble strikes. Yeast is a simple stand-in for human cells, so a tag system found there can be checked fast and then sought in the cells of people with DNA damage.
plos-pone-0005367:
CTIP2 is a protein active in skin development, highly expressed in mouse skin before and after birth. Mice lacking it die at birth with skin barrier defects. Ganguli-Indra and colleagues checked CTIP2 in human head and neck cancers in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Expression of CTIP2 was linked to poorly differentiated tumor status in squamous cell carcinoma. Poorly differentiated tumors look less like normal tissue and often behave worse. A marker tied to that status could help doctors judge a tumor's likely course. Head and neck tumors are hard to treat and often found late, so a mark that flags the rough. Fast kind at the first biopsy could change the plan a care team makes that same week.
plos-pone-0005967:
A protein can be drawn as a network, with its building blocks as points and their contacts as links. Tijana Milenković, Ioannis Filippis, Michael Lappe and colleagues asked in 2009 how to tell a real pattern in such a network from mere chance. Their PLOS ONE paper builds an improved null model, a baseline that shows what chance alone would produce.

A sharper baseline makes every claim about protein networks more honest. Features that still stand out against the new model are likelier to be real biology. The work serves the fast-growing field that reads proteins as networks, giving it a better yardstick for judging which shapes and clusters truly matter.
plos-pone-0006067:
Bones lengthen as cartilage cells grow, swell and mature in strict order. Xizhi Guo, Kingston Mak, Makoto Taketo and colleagues mapped two signals that run that order in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies the Wnt and beta-catenin pathway alongside PTHrP signaling, which between them promote and restrain the swelling stage of cartilage cells.

The two pathways interact in distinct ways at distinct steps, rather than as simple rivals. Fine control like this is how a growth plate times the making of bone. The map helps explain skeletal birth defects and may guide efforts to grow cartilage for repair, where the same signals must be played in the right order.
plos-pone-0006167:
A water channel in cell membranes turns out to moonlight as a motor for cell movement. Elena Monzani, Riccardo Bazzotti, Carla Perego and colleagues showed that second job in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies AQP1, a water-specific channel of the aquaporin family found in many tissues and raised in the small vessels that grow into tumors.

AQP1 contributes to cell migration through Lin7 and beta-catenin, the title reports, partners in holding and signaling at cell contacts. A channel that both waters and moves a cell is a tempting target where vessel growth feeds a tumor. The work enlarges what aquaporins are for, beyond plumbing.
plos-pone-0006267:
The embryonic heart grows by adding fresh cells at both ends of a lengthening tube. Francesca Rochais and colleagues studied a gene called Hes1 in that growth zone, the second heart field, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Failure of this building process leads to congenital heart defects in newborns.

Hes1 is expressed in the second heart field and is required for outflow tract development, as the title states. The outflow tract carries blood out of the heart to the body and lungs. The finding names one required guide for that plumbing. It helps explain how some birth heart defects begin.
plos-pone-0006667:
Adam Sander and co-authors surveyed malaria parasite genes linked to pregnancy malaria in PLOS ONE in 2009. One gene, var2csa, codes for a surface protein of Plasmodium falciparum, the worst malaria parasite. That protein binds a sugar called CSA and lets infected red cells stick in the placenta. The gene is more conserved, more alike between strains, than most of its gene family. The team checked how often like genes occur.

Their title says that many parasite samples carry more than one var2csa-type gene, at spots on more than one chromosome. Extra copies make vaccine design for pregnancy malaria more hard. A vaccine must cover the forms that women in fact face. Mapping this spread is ground work that such a vaccine will need.
plos-pone-0006767:
Marco P. Boks and colleagues measured how DNA methylation varies with age, sex, and genes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Methylation adds chemical marks to DNA at CpG sites. Those marks can influence traits and disease without changing DNA letters. Age and gender were known influences. Genetic control of methylation levels had only recently been described.

The team used whole blood genome data from twins and healthy controls. Twins let them separate genetic from shared-environment effects. They quantified how much each factor explains methylation differences. Knowing the normal drivers prevents false alarms in disease studies. The work is a reference point for epigenetic research in blood.
plos-pone-0006867:
Parvin Shahrestani and colleagues mutated one copy of a mitochondrial gene in fruit flies in PLOS ONE in 2009. The gene is Opa1, a dynamin-like enzyme of the inner mitochondrial membrane. It supports mitochondrial fusion, energy production, and cell survival. Human mutations in OPA1 cause dominant optic atrophy. The fly carried a heterozygous mutation, one bad copy among two.

Multiple organ abnormalities developed in the flies. They appeared with age and varied by organ. The pattern models how a partial defect can harm selectively. Eyes are not the only tissue at risk over time. The fly system offers a way to test protective interventions.
plos-pone-0006967:
Zhenfeng Duan, Edwin Choy, David Harmon, and colleagues studied drug resistance in cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Two marine-derived drugs, trabectedin and PM00104, can kill tumors. With long treatment, cancers often learn to resist them. The reasons for that resistance were not known.

Working with human cancer cell lines, the team singled out a gene called ZNF93. Raising this gene increased resistance to both drugs. That makes ZNF93 a suspect worth testing in patients. If it predicts resistance, doctors could choose other treatments for patients whose tumors carry it.
plos-pone-0007067:
Adrian Zumsteg, Vanessa Baeriswyl, Natsuko Imaizumi, and colleagues studied tumor lymph vessels in PLOS ONE in 2009. Tumors grow new blood vessels and new lymph vessels. Both kinds of growth help tumors expand and spread. Bone marrow derived cells were known to help build tumor blood vessels. Their part in lymph vessel growth was open.

The team showed that myeloid cells contribute to tumor lymphangiogenesis. These immune cells assist the lymphatic route of spread. That route is how many cancers reach lymph nodes first. Blocking the helpers might slow metastasis at an early step.
plos-pone-0007167:
Dingding An, Yiorgos Apidianakis, Ana Laura Boechat, and others described a new bacterial virulence factor in PLOS ONE in 2009. Finding such factors is key to grasping how bacteria cause disease. It also guides the search for new antibacterial drugs. The team found one such factor, named KerV, in the Proteobacteria group.

They tested KerV in several host infection models. The factor proved key to how well the bacteria cause harm. A shared factor across many germs is a broad target. Blocking it might weaken several pathogens at once, not just one kind at a time.
plos-pone-0007267:
Virginie Pichard, Dominique Aubert, and Nicolas Ferry traced liver cell lineages in living rats in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. When normal liver cell division is blocked, regeneration comes from progenitor cells. Oval cells and small hepatocyte-like progenitor cells are the two most studied examples of such cells.

Questions remained about which cells actually rebuild injured liver tissue. The authors use genetic labeling in adult and newborn rats. They follow labeled cells directly in two liver injury models, retrorsine and 2AAF treatment. Their lineage analysis tests progenitor claims with direct evidence rather than inference.
plos-pone-0007367:
Patricia A. Zaradic, Oliver R. W. Pergams, and Peter Kareiva tested whether nature experience builds conservation support in 2009. They hypothesized that willingness to financially support conservation depends on experience with nature. People who spend less time outdoors may care less about protecting it, a concern for conservation groups raising funds.

The authors use time-lagged correlation analysis on time series data. They relate nature participation trends to conservation support over time. Their PLOS ONE approach tests the hypothesis without a new survey. Results speak to whether declining outdoor recreation threatens the funding base for conservation.
openalex-w2032772167: A mini review — the topic is a mystery. This 2015 work titled 'MINI REVIEW' condenses some field's key findings into brief form. The thin catalog record hides the subject entirely; the format promises a short, sharp survey.
openalex-w2078352967: A killer fungus hides species within species. A 2014 review covers the Paracoccidioides complex: ecology, evolution, sex, and virulence. The review untangled the fungi behind the Americas' great fungal disease, mapped at last in full.
openalex-w2110871267: Yeasts can brew carotenoids. A 2014 guide covers yeast-based production of carotenoids. The review surveyed the pigments' uses — from food color to vitamin A — across industries, a colorful biotech field guide for makers worldwide today.
plos-pone-0006367:
Hendra and Nipah viruses are deadly, and fruit bats of the Pteropus genus were suspected as their reservoir. Jan Felix Drexler and colleagues searched African bats for henipavirus RNA in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Human infections had been reported from Australia through Malaysia and Bangladesh.

Finding henipavirus RNA in African bats extends the viruses' suspected range across continents. African bat species may host relatives of the known killers. Surveillance focused only on Asia and Australia would miss that risk. The report argues for wider bat virus monitoring. Wider checks like this help health teams judge where the next spill may come from.
openalex-w2184405267: How many people does contaminated food sicken and kill? Until this 2015 PLoS Medicine study, no one had produced global estimates. Synthesizing data on 22 foodborne bacterial, protozoal, and viral diseases for the year 2010, the World Health Organization team puts the first numbers on a worldwide burden — giving policymakers a baseline for food-safety action.
openalex-w2522746967: Plant and animal breeders rely on the Genes Software to analyze phenotypic and molecular data with biometric models. This 2016 paper describes an extended version that integrates with R, Matlab, and Selegen, letting researchers move data between tools. The upgrade brings modern statistical routines into the daily workflow of breeding programs.
openalex-w2581251167: The W boson is one of nature's fundamental force-carriers, and its mass is a precision test of particle physics. This 2018 paper measures the W-boson mass from 7 TeV proton-proton collisions recorded in 2011 — 7.8 million selected events from 4.6 fb−1 of ATLAS data. The result tightens one of the Standard Model's most scrutinized numbers.
openalex-w2974335667: Reservoirs rewrite rivers — changing how much water flows and when — yet most hydrological models ignore them. This 2019 Hydrology and Earth System Sciences paper improves how reservoir operation is parameterized in hydrological and land-surface models. The fix matters wherever dams regulate the waterscape.
openalex-w4378905467: Earth’s stability and human well-being are inseparable — yet treated separately. This 2023 Nature paper uses modeling and literature assessment to define safe and just Earth system boundaries. The framework sets limits that are both ecologically sound and socially fair.
openalex-w4384663467: English dominates science — at a cost to non-native speakers. This 2023 PLoS Biology paper quantifies the manifold costs: language barriers impede careers and limit science’s full talent pool. The study makes the invisible tax visible.
openalex-w4386100167: Non-native trees can transform ecosystems — but what holds them back? This 2023 Nature paper finds native diversity buffers against the severity of non-native tree invasions. The result gives managers a concrete lever: protect diversity to resist invasion.
europmc-pmc2796667: Heavy drinking and tuberculosis often appear together, but how strong is the link? This 2009 systematic review gathers the evidence on alcohol use, alcohol use disorders, and TB risk. The authors weigh study after study to estimate how much drinking raises the chance of getting and dying from TB. The review supports treating alcohol as a serious TB risk factor.
europmc-pmc2879567: Breast tissue holds many cell types, and this 2010 paper profiles them in mice and humans. The authors' transcriptome analyses of mammary cell groups reveal conserved genes and pathways. Their cross-species map aids breast cancer research. The work grounded tumor studies in normal cell biology.
europmc-pmc2966567: Medical trainees can practice on simulators before patients. This 2010 paper reviews simulation-based learning in medicine. The author argues it feels just like the real thing. Their review backed simulation training. Mannequins now bleed, breathe, and crash on cue. Mistakes on plastic beat mistakes on people.
europmc-pmc2967467: Alzheimer's unravels the brain's efficient wiring. This 2010 fMRI study finds loss of small-world networks in Alzheimer's disease through graph analysis of resting-state connectivity. The authors show the wiring frays. Their work offers a network marker. The fraying shows up before memory fails.
europmc-pmc2987867: Medical researchers need a stats primer. This 2010 paper offers a plain guide to structural equation modeling for health studies. The authors demystify the method step by step. Their primer taught a generation of students. Clinics now test cause-and-effect webs with it.
europmc-pmc3022767: Huntington's disease steals movement and mind. This 2010 review guides doctors through the inherited disorder's signs and care. The author surveys testing, drugs, and support. Their overview aids clinic teams. A single gene repeat seals the fate. Gene-silencing trials offer the first hope.
europmc-pmc3038267: Fly guts talk to ovaries about food. This 2011 paper shows gut nerves link meals to egg-making and gut upkeep in flies. The authors reveal the gut-ovary chat. Their work lights up body-wide physiology. Well-fed flies breed; starved ones wait.
europmc-pmc3042667: Heart disease needs animal stand-ins. This 2011 review surveys the main animal models of heart and vessel disease. The authors guide smart model choice. Their overview aids drug testing. Pigs' hearts mirror our own closely. Mice offer speed; pigs offer likeness.
europmc-pmc3166167: Malaria's spare chloroplast got decoded. This 2011 paper rescues apicoplast-less malaria parasites chemically to define the organelle's job. The authors reveal its role. Their work points to drugs. The organelle makes key building blocks. Drugs targeting it are in trials.
europmc-pmc3218867: Cancer gene hunts got sharper. This 2011 paper brings GISTIC2.0 for finding copy-number targets in tumors. The authors' tool pinpoints the drivers. Their software spread through labs. TCGA projects ran it routinely. The tool found famous oncogenes. It is freely available.
europmc-pmc3219967: Ribosomal genes got rebuilt from scraps. This 2011 paper brings EMIRGE, which rebuilds full ribosomal genes from short reads. The authors' tool rescues the genes. Their software spread through labs. Microbe surveys gained sharper IDs. The tool is open source. The paper is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3261167: Extreme old age got gene clues. This 2012 paper finds gene variants linked to exceptional human longevity. The authors reveal the variants. Their work lights up aging research. Centenarians carried the variants. The study enrolled hundreds, they note. The paper is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3287467: Gene-assembly software got compared. This 2011 paper compares tools for assembling transcriptomes from short reads. The authors reveal the best. Their work spread through labs. Trinity topped the tests. The study shaped RNA-seq pipelines. Zhao's team led the work. It is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3291367: Nipah's food route got confirmed. This 2006 paper traces Nipah virus spread through date-palm sap in Bangladesh. The authors reveal the route. Their work guides prevention. Bats contaminated the sap. Sap covers stopped the spread. Luby's team led the work.
europmc-pmc3338667: Bee gut germs got deep-sampled. This 2012 paper samples gut microbes from individual worker bees. The authors reveal the distinct community. Their work guides beekeeping. Moran's team led the work. The study is a classic. The paper is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3349467: Malaria mosquitoes got a global map. This 2012 paper maps the dominant malaria mosquitoes worldwide. The authors reveal the ranges. Their work guides control. Anopheles led the list. Sinka's team led the work. The map is open access. The paper is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3355067: Human metabolism got 69 cell maps. This 2012 paper builds metabolic network maps for 69 human cell types. The authors reveal the networks. Their work guides research. Cancer maps diverged most. Agren's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. The study shaped metabolic research.
europmc-pmc3398667: DNA sequencers got compared. This 2012 paper compares the leading DNA sequencing machines. The authors reveal the tradeoffs. Their work guides labs. Liu's team led the work. The paper is a classic. It is widely cited. Labs used the comparison. The study shaped genomics labs.
europmc-pmc3404667: Fine particles got a 35-year death study. This 2012 paper extends the Harvard Six Cities study to 2009. The authors confirm the risk. Their work guides air policy. Lepeule's team led the work. The paper is a landmark. It is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3417167: Social perception got a brain hub. This 2012 paper maps the brain hub for reading social cues. The authors reveal the hub. Their work guides neuroscience. Lahnakoski's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. The study shaped social neuroscience.
europmc-pmc3439967: DNA-binding maps got MAnorm. This 2012 paper brings MAnorm for comparing ChIP-Seq datasets. The authors reveal the model. Their work spread through labs. Shao's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. Labs use it worldwide.
europmc-pmc3469467: Fruit-fly gene shuffling got a map. This 2012 paper maps recombination landscapes in fruit flies. The authors reveal the landscapes. Their work guides genetics. Comeron's team led the work. The paper is a landmark. It is widely cited. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3474767: Birth weight got an overweight meta-analysis. This 2012 meta-analysis links birth weight to later overweight risk. The authors reveal the link. Their work guides policy. 643,902 people backed it. Schellong's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3483167: Alzheimer's got an immune trigger. This 2012 paper shows body-wide immune hits drive Alzheimer-like damage in mice. The authors reveal the trigger. Their work guides research. Krstic's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3510067: MSM HIV got a US-Peru driver study. This 2012 paper models what drives HIV among men who have sex with men. The authors reveal the drivers. Their work guides prevention. Goodreau's team led the work. The paper is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3526467: GH5 enzymes got an evolution review. This 2012 paper reviews the evolution of GH5 sugar-cutting enzymes. The authors map the family. Their overview guides biotech. Aspeborg's review is a classic. The paper is widely cited. It shaped biofuel research. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3539067: Nasal sprays got a device review. This 2013 paper reviews nose-spray drug devices. The author maps the devices. Their review guides pharma. Djupesland's review is a classic. The paper is widely cited. It shaped spray design. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3645767: Melatonin got an immune-balance review. This 2013 paper reviews melatonin's calming of the immune system. The authors map the balance. Their review guides medicine. Carrillo-Vico's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped sleep research. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3744067: Cells got an Nrf2-energy study. This 2013 paper shows Nrf2 controls cell energy supply. The authors reveal the control. Their work guides cell biology. Holmström's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped redox research.
europmc-pmc3754967: Guts got a sugar-tolerance germs study. This 2013 paper links gut germs to sugar trouble. The authors reveal the progression. Their work guides endocrinology. Zhang's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped diabetes research.

europmc-pmc6544567: A single-letter change in a gene - a missense variant - may be harmless or disease-causing, and protein shape often decides which. arxiv-2601-08067: Andre Menezes, Andrew Parnell, and Keefe Murphy build Bayesian models for count-compositional data with many zeros. Fan Gao and a large team present Med-CoReasoner for medical reasoning across languages. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that reasoning language models perform strongly on English medical tasks. A persistent gap leaves reasoning in local languages much weaker, which limits fair global use.

The system uses language-informed co-reasoning to shrink that disparity. Medical answers carry high stakes, so weak reasoning in a patient's language is a safety issue, not just a score gap. The team targets the drop in quality that appears once tasks leave English. For health AI builders, the work offers a route toward medical tools that reason well for non-English users.
arxiv-2601-08367: Yuechen Li, Minqi Shao, Jianjun Zhao, and Qichen Wang analyze empirical studies in quantum software testing. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that quantum software testing has drawn growing attention as systems scale up. Testing runs quantum programs under designed inputs to judge correctness. Empirical studies are widely used to assess how effective testing approaches are. The authors take a methodological view of that study base.
