arxiv-2601-08567:
Jun Jiang, Cong-Feng Qiao, and Yu-Han Zhao hunt for a proposed particle called X(17). Their 2026 arXiv paper addresses the beryllium-8 anomaly reported by the Atomki experiments. That anomaly can be explained by a hypothetical X(17) boson.

In the hypothesis, the boson interacts with electrons through a vector plus or minus axial-vector interaction. Such an interaction shape changes where and how the particle should appear in other experiments. A confirmed new boson near 17 megaelectronvolts would break the Standard Model. The hunt matters because several labs have chased the anomaly with mixed results, and a clear theory target sharpens each test.
arxiv-2601-07567:
Eimear Byrne and colleagues measure how much information can leak from a secure network code. Their 2026 preprint studies secure linear network coding built on nested rank-metric codes. In network coding, intermediate nodes mix data packets rather than just forwarding them. An adversary may watch a subset of network links and try to learn the message.

The authors show that leakage is captured by a conditional rank function. That function belongs to a representable q-polymatroid tied to the underlying code pair. In plain terms, an abstract structure counts exactly what an eavesdropper can learn. Such results help designers prove a code leaks nothing beyond a set limit. The paper serves coding theorists working on secure communication over shared networks.
arxiv-2601-07667:
Rei Taniguchi and colleagues trim the memory that large language models use while generating text. The key-value cache stores past tokens so the model need not recompute them. Long contexts make that cache a major cost. Layer-wise token pruning keeps only a subset of tokens at chosen layers. Their 2026 preprint studies how to pick which layers do the pruning.

Choosing layers adaptively matters because layers play different roles. Some layers need broad context; others can work from a few key tokens. The authors propose adaptive layer selection for this pruning scheme. Done well, pruning cuts memory and latency with little quality loss. The work speaks to engineers serving large models under tight hardware budgets. It treats layer choice as part of the method, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2601-07767:
Jiawei Wang and colleagues test whether language models act on the confidence they express. Models can produce surprisingly sophisticated estimates of their own uncertainty. It remains unclear whether that stated confidence connects to their reasoning or decisions. Their 2026 preprint introduces RiskEval, a framework for this question. RiskEval checks whether models adjust when to abstain as error penalties change.

A model that truly uses its confidence should refuse more when mistakes cost more. If its answers stay fixed while its words sound cautious, the confidence is decoration. Such tests matter for deploying models in medicine, law, and finance. Abstention is often the safest action a model can take. The paper speaks to scholars evaluating calibration and trust in large language models.
arxiv-2601-08667:
Tom Garcia-Sanchez studies a random tree that grows from a single root point. Points fall at random in space. Each point links to the next point that sits close to the root. In this way a tree forms, with paths that run out from the root. The key ask is how straight those paths are.

He shows the tree is straight in all sizes of space, not just on a flat plane. Straight here means the paths do not bend far from a direct line. The proof adds to what we know about random shapes in space. A reader with a taste for chance and shape gets a neat, clean result. It also helps work on random nets that grow from one hub.
arxiv-2601-09167:
Sangam Balchandar Reddy and three co-authors ask how hard a guard task on a graph is to solve. The task is global Roman domination. Each point gets a tag of zero, one, or two. A zero point must sit next to a two point, as a town with no guard must sit next to a strong post. The guard must span the whole graph, not one part.

The team maps the hard grade of this task on graph types. Such maps tell us if a fast true solve can exist, or if we must use near best picks. A reader in graph work gets a place for this task in the hard task zoo. It guides what solve tools to try on real nets.
arxiv-2601-09267:
Satoru Hayami and Kazuki Okigami study spin forms with more than one wave in a one way metal. In such a metal, charge flows in a line of atoms. Spins can line in a spiral wave. They can also line in a stag form, up down up down. Each form has its own wave span. Set both at once, and they can cross to make rich new forms.

The team works out what forms that cross can make. The new forms mix wave spans that no turn rule ties. That mix is the odd part: past multi wave forms used spans tied by turns of the crystal. A reader in magnet work gets new forms that may hide in plain line metals.
arxiv-2601-09367:
Aidana Aidynkyzy and three co-authors test how well large language models extract relations from clinical text. Their 2026 arXiv paper is a bilingual evaluation covering English and Turkish. Relation extraction means finding stated links, such as which drug treats which condition, inside medical writing.

Work in this area has centered on English, because annotated clinical data in other languages is scarce. The authors present what they describe as the first full bilingual evaluation of its kind. Comparing the two languages shows where models trained mostly on English fall short. The results point to what Turkish clinical text still needs: data and methods of its own.
arxiv-2601-09667:
Zhiyuan Hu and a large team let language model agents learn at test time instead of in training. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents MATTRL, multi-agent test-time reinforcement learning for reasoning. Multi-agent systems gain robustness from diverse members that check each other.

Training such teams jointly is costly and unstable: teammates keep changing, and rewards are sparse and noisy. MATTRL instead feeds structured text experience into the team's deliberation while it works. The team adapts on the job, without new gradient training. Test-time learning could make agent teams cheaper to field and quicker to improve.
arxiv-2601-09867:
Yifan Zhang and Yishan Yang enlist ambient radio energy to guard wireless messages. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents AmbShield, which uses ambient backscatter devices against passive eavesdroppers. Eavesdropping threatens privacy most where devices are too weak for heavy cryptography.

Physical layer security uses channel randomness and direction to confine a signal to its intended receiver. Standard tricks like beamforming, artificial noise, or smart surfaces cost power or demand precise timing and channel data. AmbShield instead rides on backscatter devices that reflect ambient waves. Low-cost shielding would suit the tiny sensors now spread through homes and farms.
arxiv-2601-10067:
Hung Vinh Tran and co authors cut the cost of training a shop aid. Such aids guess what a user will like from item traits. They serve vast web shops with wide tastes. To keep up, they must train on huge data, again and again. That costs time and power.

The team picks a small core set to train on. The pick is wise to noise. Bad or off rows are kept out of the core. A small clean core can train a model near as well as the full set. The work aims to keep grades high while the train bill drops.
arxiv-2601-10367:
Daniela Aguirre Salazar, Firas Moatemri, and Tatiana Tatarenko learn game rules from acts in two by two games. Such games have two players with two moves each. From acts alone, one can try to infer what each player seeks. That task is named inverse learning.

The team give two tools for the task. One fits a shared chance form of play at rest. One fits how players adapt over time by a logit rule. They test the tools on forged data first. They then use them in a traffic sim. There, drivers act as players at each cross.
arxiv-2601-10567:
Laura Ferrarotti and co authors argue that AI group acts need a new lens. Teams of language model agents can act as a crowd. Their joint acts can help or harm at a wide scale. Past work oft reads a crowd from each agent on its own. The team say that read is too thin.

They call for an interactionist lens. In that lens, acts grow from how agents meet and sway each other. Norms and cascades form in the play twixt agents. The paper sets out why this lens is a must. It also maps the risks and gains such crowds bring to society.
arxiv-2601-10667:
Tobin A. Driscoll and Yuxing Zhou solve a numerical snag in working with rational functions. Fast methods exist to build rational approximations in two forms, barycentric and continued fraction. But taking derivatives of those approximations can go unstable. Small errors blow up, and the computed slopes turn to noise.

The authors present the first stable methods for derivatives in the barycentric form. One method gets all derivatives in linear time. Stable slopes matter wherever fitted curves are used for rates, sensitivities, or control. The paper gives numerical analysts tools they can trust on real data, not just on paper.
arxiv-2601-10967:
Kyrho Corum, Renier Mendoza, Victoria May P. Mendoza, and Arrianne Crystal Velasco build optimization models for dengue control with Wolbachia. Dengue is spread by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes and strikes millions each year. In the Philippines, its yearly economic cost is put near 17 billion pesos. Releasing Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes can cut transmission, since the bacteria block the virus.

The models balance economic cost against disease impact. Releases cost money and effort; cases cost health and income. An optimum plan says where and how much to release for the best trade. The work serves health planners in dengue-prone regions who must spend limited budgets where they save the most illness.
arxiv-2601-12267: Alejandro González Nevado claims a proof of the generalized Lax conjecture by topological means. The conjecture links rigidly convex sets to determinants of symmetric linear pencils. RZ polynomials are real polynomials with set zero traits tied to those sets. His route uses compactness, convexity, and determinantal deformations. He builds determinants of large pencils as products of approximating linear forms grow. A proof would close a long open problem in convex algebraic geometry. The work sets out that topological case in full.
arxiv-2601-11267:
Shuning Tan and five coauthors map pairing states in a Hubbard model. Their 2026 preprint uses constrained-path quantum Monte Carlo runs. The model adds a pull between sites next to each other. Spin-linked hopping can favor one way over its mirror.

The team scans the ground-state map across two key knobs. One knob is the strength of the pull between neighbors. The other is the size of the spin-linked hopping bias. The fill of the lattice sits near 0.85 in these runs. From that map they read where odd pairing wins. The title names it oriented triplet p-wave pairing. Such states are of strong interest for exotic superconductors.
arxiv-2601-11367:
Markus Frembs, Cihan Okay, and Ho Yiu Chung rule out a class of quantum gains. Their 2026 preprint deals with linear constraint systems. Such systems set equations that answers must all meet. Some have quantum answers but no classical ones at all.

Measurement-based quantum computation is the source in this study. In that model, measurement on a set state does the work. Contextuality of the input state is a key resource there. A strong form of it yields the odd algebraic links. Those links can make classical answers fail the equations. The team shows no such quantum answers arise from one route. That route is monomial MBQC in odd prime dimension. The no-go result trims where advantage can be claimed.
arxiv-2601-11567:
Vanessa D'Amario and five coauthors grade small medical models beyond accuracy. Their 2026 preprint studies pediatric endocrinology as the test field. Small open-source medical LLMs promise low-resource deployment. They also widen access where big models cannot run.

Evaluation of such models often stops at accuracy alone. Multiple choice question scores are the usual yardstick. Consistency, robustness, and reasoning behavior go unmeasured. A model can score well yet answer unsteadily in clinic use. The team measures stability as a first-class trait. Pediatric endocrinology gives a focused, expert test domain. Safer small models need such broader checks before use.
arxiv-2601-13367:
Federico Carollo and Sascha Wald show how random resets can make a quantum path recall its past. A reset snaps a system back to a set start state at random times. Such rules draw care for three gains. They can hold a system in a steady non balance state. They can grow links in systems whose parts do not talk. They can also give best search plans.

With a fixed reset chance, the path is Markovian, with no memory of its past. Much less was known when reset chance shifts. Carollo and Wald show that resets can in fact birth non Markov acts, where past does sway what comes next. That widens how resets can be used to steer quantum acts.
arxiv-2601-13567:
Xianghui Cao and co-authors sum non perturbative pion gifts to the nucleon flavour gap in a light front frame. The gap is the known odd split of sea quarks in a nucleon, with more anti down than anti up. Perturbative sums miss its size. Pions in the cloud around a nucleon are a lead suspect.

Their frame is light front Hamiltonian effective field theory. It grows the state in Fock sectors, so a bare nucleon, a nucleon plus a pion, and more can each add their share. The pion links are set by a scalar form of chiral theory. The same frame treats the deuteron. Such sums test if the pion cloud tale holds in full.
arxiv-2601-12767:
Beniamino Hadj-Amar and Jack Jewson put forward a way to pick key variables with less faith in a full model. The Bayesian route to this task is strong and well liked. It builds in a bias for short lists and states how unsure it is. Its picks can be sound and work well on small samples.

True doubt scores need the model to be right, though. When the model is wrong, its picks and scores can mislead. Their quasi Bayesian route keeps the style but drops the full model. It is framed as model choice with no model at all. The work serves fields where all models are known to be rough. Health and social data are two such fields.
arxiv-2601-13767:
Arjun Sobnack and Peter Topping prove a new Harnack inequality for shrinking curves in 2026. Curve shortening flow moves a curve inward, faster where it bends more. In 1995, Hamilton proved a Harnack inequality for convex solutions of mean curvature flow. Convexity means the curve bulges one way, with no dents.

Sobnack and Topping prove an alternative Harnack inequality for the curve case. Their version needs no assumption of convexity at all. Harnack bounds link values of a solution at distinct times and places. Dropping the convexity need widens where the bound can be used.
arxiv-2601-13967:
Hongyu Cheng proves a spread bound for waves on a one-dimensional lattice in 2026. The equation is the Klein-Gordon equation with a quasi-periodic potential. Dispersive estimates bound how fast solutions spread and decay over time. Such bounds play a pivotal role in the long-term behavior of nonlinear equations.

They are crucial for well-posedness, whether a problem has stable solutions at all. Cheng proves solutions follow the dispersive estimate in this lattice case. The potential must be quasi-periodic with Diophantine frequencies, and close to positive constants. The result aids the study of waves in patterned media. The bound holds for a wide class of such waves. It gives later work on long-time trends a firm base to stand on.
arxiv-2601-14267:
Pouria Mortezaagha, Joseph Shaw, Bowen Sun, and Arya Rahgozar address a slow task in medical research in this 2026 paper. Teams that sum up trial evidence must pull key facts from full-text papers. The facts cover methods, lab work, and outcomes. They sit inside complex PDFs, mixed with multi-column text, tables, figures, and captions.

Pulling those facts out by hand is slow and error-prone. At the scale of modern systematic reviews, hand work is close to impractical. The team built a schema-constrained AI tool for the job. A schema fixes the exact fields to fill. Their design aims at extraction that can be audited, so each value can be checked later.
arxiv-2601-14367:
Stephen P. Schmidt and Kevin C. Schlaufman revisit the oldest problem in exoplanet astrophysics in this 2026 paper. Hot Jupiters are giant planets on very tight orbits. How they got there is still debated. If they formed in place or drifted in through the disk, they should arrive a few million years after their stars form.

Other paths are far slower. Planet-planet scattering or Kozai-Lidov oscillations can pump up a planet's eccentricity, then tidal damping shrinks its orbit. That route may take a billion years or more. The authors' title states their claim: most hot Jupiters stayed cool giant planets for more than one billion years.
arxiv-2601-14467:
Nikolas H. Claussen, Fridtjof Brauns, and Boris I. Shraiman study living tissue mechanics in this 2026 paper. Inert materials strain first, then push back. Living cells are distinct: molecular motors generate forces independently of elastic strain. The big question is how local active forces become large-scale shape. A second question asks what mechanical properties the resulting living matter has.

The team works inside the active tension network model for the mechanics of two-dimensional epithelia, sheets of cells. They coarse-grain the model, smoothing fine detail into a larger-scale picture. Their tool is discrete conformal geometry. Readers get a route from cell-level forces to tissue-level form.
arxiv-2601-14567:
Roland R. Rodriguez, Jr proposes a naming scheme for AI agents in this 2026 paper. Multi-agent systems face a fundamental architectural flaw: agent identity is bound to network location. When agents migrate between providers, scale across instances, or federate across organizations, URI-based identity schemes break. References snap, audit trails fragment, and centralized coordination becomes a must.

Rodriguez proposes an Agent Identity URI scheme that is topology-independent. Identity would stay fixed no matter where the agent runs. The scheme pairs naming with capability-based discovery, so agents find each other by what they can do. Readers get a design for agent systems that can move without losing their names.
arxiv-2601-14667:
Yijin Zhou, Xiaoya Lu, Dongrui Liu, Junchi Yan, and Jing Shao study security for agent teams in this 2026 paper. LLM-based multi-agent systems have advanced rapidly. They have also introduced significant security vulnerabilities. Malicious influence can propagate virally through inter-agent communication. One bad agent can poison the talk of the whole team.

Conventional safeguards rely on a binary paradigm. They strictly distinguish benign agents from attack agents. That view fails to account for infected agents: benign entities converted by attack agents. The team's guard, INFA-Guard, is infection-aware. Readers get a safeguard that tracks how malice spreads through a team, not just where it starts.
arxiv-2601-14767:
M. N. Mazziotta leads a team of ten authors on a particle detector design in this 2026 paper. They present a novel compact particle identification detector based on Silicon Photomultipliers, or SiPMs. The detector is optimized to perform combined Ring-Imaging Cherenkov and Time-of-Flight measurements. Both measurements use a common photodetector layer.

The system consists of a Cherenkov radiator layer separated from a photosensitive surface equipped with SiPMs by an expansion gap. Cherenkov rings give particle speed, while timing gives flight time. Together they identify particle types, including isotopes, as the title says. The kit is small. One plane does two jobs, so the whole tool can fit in tight spots. Two tests in one pass save time. They also save room, since one plane does the work of two. Readers get a compact design that does two identification jobs with one sensor plane.
arxiv-2601-15667:
Duván Cardona works on smoothing estimates for Fourier integral operators in a 2026 arXiv paper. The linear local smoothing conjecture is a celebrated open idea from Sogge. It concerns how waves concentrate and decay. Cardona formulates a bilinear version of that conjecture. Bilinear operators handle pairs of functions at once. His version is stated for every dimension two and above.

He then proves a key implication. The linear conjecture, if true, implies his bilinear one. Such links matter in harmonic analysis. A single hard conjecture can unlock a family of results. Smoothing estimates govern how solutions of wave equations behave. They feed into broader questions about waves in complex media. The paper is aimed at specialists in the field.
arxiv-2601-15867:
Dabiao Ma, Zhiba Su, Jian Yang, and Haojun Fei detect out-of-distribution inputs in a 2026 arXiv paper. Models deployed in the real world meet data unlike their training sets. Distribution shifts can silently wreck their accuracy. Guards that flag foreign inputs are therefore essential. Their method is TV-OOD, short for total variation out-of-distribution detection. It improves on existing methods, the authors say, by a new measurement.

A total variation network estimator scores each input. It estimates the input's contribution to overall total variation. Inputs that push variation high look out of place. That signal separates them from normal data. For safety-critical deployments, a good OOD alarm is the difference between a graceful refusal and a confident error.
arxiv-2601-15967:
Mingshan Chi, Anh-Thy Bui, Pierre Lidon, and Yaocihuatl Medina Gonzalez calibrate tiny viscosity probes in a 2026 arXiv paper. Fluorescent molecular rotors report local microviscosity in complex materials. They have served as probes for decades. Their readings are relative, though. Without proper calibration, tying microviscosity to a physical parameter stays unclear. That limit sharply reduces their quantitative use. Biological media are a prime example of where the limit bites.

The team studies rotor response in ternary macromolecular mixtures. Three-component mixtures mimic crowded real fluids better than simple ones. Crowded fluids fill cells and many industrial products. A calibration that works there extends the probe's reach. Chemists who measure soft matter rely on such groundwork before trusting rotor numbers.
arxiv-2601-15167:
Francesca Randone, Romina Doz, Mirco Tribastone, and Luca Bortolussi tune probabilistic programs without drawing samples. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with programs that mix chance with code. Such programs can have both continuous and discrete parts.

The team presents DeGAS, a differentiable Gaussian approximate semantics for loopless programs. Programs run under a Gaussian-mixture meaning instead of exact chance. Sharp predicates and discrete branches get a smooth stand-in that fades away. The result is a set of closed-form expressions for the key probabilities. Those forms stay open to gradient-based optimization, with no sampling needed at all.
arxiv-2601-15267:
Yiran Hu, Huanghai Liu, and a large team survey how language models are judged for legal work. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a fast-growing use of AI. Models now support judges, aid legal practice, and serve the public with legal information.

Evaluating such models is its own problem. The authors review the challenges that legal uses raise for testing. They sort the methods used so far to grade legal performance. They then set out future directions, so the next tests can be harder to game and closer to real legal needs.
arxiv-2601-15467:
H. S. Battey and Charlotte Edgar offer a critique of a basic term in statistics. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the treatment effect, the measured impact of a treatment or policy. Two broad camps define it in rival ways.

One camp treats the effect as a parameter of a statistical model. The other treats it as a population-level difference in outcomes. That difference may be stated in counterfactual terms: outcomes under one regime versus another. The authors weigh the two positions and what each one commits its users to in practice.
arxiv-2601-16067:
Ashok Kumar and five coauthors probe a mixed oxide and its traits. Their 2026 preprint studies grains of LaV0.5Nb0.5O4, made in bulk form. The team made the stuff at two bake heats, one at 1000 and one at 1250 degrees. Swapping part of one ion for a like but larger ion shifts the build. The shift shows in the grain form and in how it shakes.

The authors check build, charge traits, shake modes and charge store traits. They link each trait to the bake heat and the ion swap. Such links help pick bake terms for a set trait. The oxide is of use where charge store and firm build count. The work adds a full trait map for this mix.
arxiv-2601-16167:
Aritro Pathak extends past work on the size drop of harmonic size. His 2026 preprint deals with zones in space of three or more dims. Each zone has a rim that is firm in the Ahlfors David sense. The rim size sits near one less than the space size. Harmonic size lives on that rim and guides wave and heat acts.

Pathak shows the size lives on a set of less size than the rim. That drop is sharp in the terms he sets. Drops of this kind shape how waves hit rough rims. They also guide heat flow near such rims. The work firms up a line begun by Azzam.
arxiv-2601-16267:
Braden Marazzo-Nowicki and coauthors fit the black hole at our galaxy heart from sharp views. Their 2026 preprint uses Event Horizon Telescope views of Sagittarius A star. The scope made the first pic of the hole shade. The source shifts fast, in less time than one view run. Fast shifts block the plain way to fill view gaps by earth spin.

The team fits a half maths model to the views in place. The model gives hole mass and fall flow traits. Fits that hold through fast shifts earn more trust. They test how well the shade size pins the mass. The work aids the read of the most near huge black hole.
arxiv-2601-16367:
Bryce Ferguson and three coauthors weigh the gap when game models miss the true case. Their 2026 preprint deals with web games played by more than one agent. Each agent may hold its own game model of the whole. Those models can part ways in key terms. Parts then act on split views of the same game.

The team sums how much that split costs in end acts. Cost marks tell when model doubt must be cut ere play. They also show which split terms hurt most in the game. Such marks guide safe play in web and trade games. The work links model flaws to real act loss.
arxiv-2601-16767:
Tao Morisaki, Atsushi Matsubayashi, Yasutoshi Makino, and Hiroyuki Shinoda make touch you can feel in mid-air. Beams of ultrasound can press on skin with no gear worn. Past work showed both buzz feels and steady push feels. The push comes from a sound spot spun in a small loop. Their 2026 preprint breaks touch into three base parts.

With three parts, many feels can be built like chords. A buzz, a push, and a third part span the set. Their tests show how to mix the parts for rich feels. Such touch could serve games, cars, and aid tools for the blind. It adds feel to screens that now give none.
arxiv-2601-17067:
Luozhou Wang and a large team ask if video bots can act as world models. Big video bots now make clips with true-seeming physics. That hint says they may hold a world model in them. Old world model tales center on state kept over time. New video bots hold no clear state at all. Their 2026 preprint bridges that gap with a two-part sort.

One part is how state gets built in the bot. The next part is how change gets rolled forth. The sort lets teams grade bots as world models. It also names what bots lack for that rank. Such grades guide bots for robots and sims.
arxiv-2601-17367:
Zecheng Tang and eight co-authors present Elastic Attention for long texts in language models. Standard attention grows in cost with the square of length. That growth blocks very long inputs. Hybrid plans mix sparse and full attention in one model. But most set the mix once and for all. Real texts vary, so a fixed mix wastes work.

Elastic Attention shifts the sparsity ratio at test time. It spends full attention where the text needs it. It saves where sparse views suffice. The result should be faster long reads with less loss. Teams that serve book-length inputs gain a flexible tool. It adapts cost to content, not just to a preset.
arxiv-2601-17467:
Jianxiong Zhang and four co-authors hunt false answers from large reasoning models. These models write long, smooth chains of thought. The chains can still end in wrong answers. That makes hallucination hard to catch by eye. Past detectors read trace text or raw hidden states. Both can latch onto surface style, not truth.

The team shapes representations by answer agreement. Reasoning paths that agree earn a shared shape. Paths that split stand apart. That structure should flag shaky answers more soundly. Trust in reasoning models needs such checks. Long thought is no proof of right thought. Their method reads the paths for what they agree on.
arxiv-2601-17767:
Rajan Das Gupta, Xiaobin Wu, Xun Liu, and Jiaqi He build a new tool for spotting heart disease. Their 2026 preprint names the system HyCARD-Net. Heart disease is the top cause of death in the world, so early and sound detection matters a great deal. Older models often fail when data sets differ from each other or when body signals follow complex patterns.

HyCARD-Net mixes two kinds of methods in one frame. Deep learning parts, named CNN and LSTM, learn patterns from the data. Classic methods, named KNN and XGBoost, add their own strengths. A voting step then joins the views of all four parts. The aim is a diagnosis tool that holds up across mixed data.
arxiv-2601-18167: Mijia Lai and Zixiao Wang establish a necessary condition for the logarithmic Minkowski problem in higher dimensions. Their 2026 preprint extends a condition first proposed for the two-dimensional case by Liu, Lu, Sun, and Xiong. The new result also refines the subspace concentration condition. The Minkowski problem asks when a given measure comes from the surface of a convex body.
arxiv-2601-18967:
Julio A. Méndez-Zavaleta, Efraín Rojas, and José Joaquín Suárez-Garibay revisit a black hole with quantum roots. A known variant of the BTZ black hole was first built in a gravity theory where quantum jitter of matter shaped the result. The team asks whether plain classical physics can give the same shape.

They show it can: the same form, marked by log shaped falloff far away, solves Einstein gravity paired with a certain nonlinear electric field theory. It is the unique steady answer in that setup. The match hints that some quantum looking effects may have plain classical twins.
arxiv-2601-19367:
Bilel Sefsaf and six co-authors teach a learning agent to tune encrypted computing. Fully homomorphic encryption lets software compute on data while it stays encrypted, a prized privacy tool. Its high cost is the catch: encrypted operations run far slower than plain ones.

Their system, CHEHAB RL, uses reinforcement learning to optimize how such computations are laid out. Choices like how numbers are packed change the bill by large factors. An agent that learns those choices could make private computing far cheaper. That would widen its everyday use in banks, hospitals, and cloud tools that cannot see raw data.
arxiv-2601-19467:
Eric Alsmann, Lowejatan Noori, and Martin Lange measure what state space models can and cannot say. State space models have risen as a rival to transformers for language tasks. To grade their power, the team reads them through temporal logic, a formal language for patterns over time.

They study fragments and extensions of linear temporal logic over finite traces. If a model class matches a logic fragment, then tasks past that fragment are beyond it by proof, not by hunch. Such maps help builders pick architectures with open eyes about what each can express.
arxiv-2601-19667:
Adam Remaki and four colleagues work on linking medical terms in text to the right entries in a knowledge base. This task, biomedical entity linking, connects a mention in a note to a standard concept. Supervised systems need many examples labelled by experts. Such annotation is slow and expensive, so training data stays scarce.

Their framework, SynCABEL, uses large language models to create synthetic training examples. The examples are rich in context and cover all candidate concepts in the target base. That gives broad supervision with no manual labelling. Models trained on the synthetic data can then link real mentions. The work attacks the data bottleneck that holds back medical language tools.
arxiv-2601-20667:
Qian Gao, Ruikang Zhong, and Yuanwei Liu build a deep learning solution, in three stages, for beamforming in integrated sensing and communication systems. In their setup, a base station communicates with several users while also performing target detection. The design problem is to maximize the total communication rate.

The maximization is subject to a transmit power limit and minimum sensing rates for the users. Splitting the solution into three stages makes a coupled problem learnable. Systems that sense and talk through one station are a pillar of planned sixth-generation networks, from traffic monitoring to smart factories.
arxiv-2601-18567:
Sergio Ortolani and eight colleagues study an old star group that sits in the thick core of our galaxy. Star groups of this kind are the best marks left of the first build of the galaxy. Most marks of that age have been wiped by hits and slow change. This group is rich in heavy stuff for its age, which makes it a prize clue.

The group is named Tonantzintla 2. Its stars hold a mix that hints at a fast, rich birth in the young galaxy. The team read its light to chart its age, its stuff, and its path. Each such group adds a stone to the tale of how the core was built. A rich old group in the core backs the view that the core grew fast and early. More such finds would let staff draw that tale in finer strokes.
arxiv-2601-18867:
Katsumasa Nakayama and Kei Suzuki tie two tales of a faint push that shows up when a thing is held in a small box. In one tale, the push comes from a chain of spins that point up or down. In the next tale, it comes from a sea of bits that fill the box. A famed map turns spins into such bits one by one. The pair use that map to show the two tales are one.

They work on two famed spin chains, one with a field across it and one with fields in two ways. For both, all the small-box shifts in the spin tale match the box push in the bit tale. That match is neat: it says the map holds not just for the bulk, but for the faint edge terms too. Such ties help staff trust maps.
arxiv-2601-21167:
Shuai Liu, Alireza Bakhtiari, Alex Ayoub, Botao Hao, and Csaba Szepesvári study how to pick the best option when each try also gives context. Their setting is a bandit problem, where choices must be made one by one with partial feedback. They judge success by simple regret, which measures the quality of the final pick.

For the logistic version of the problem, no such guarantees were known before. The authors build the first algorithm with a proven regret rate for this case. They borrow ideas from the simpler linear case and from careful self-tuning analysis. The result extends bandit theory to a widely used model of yes-or-no outcomes.
arxiv-2601-21367:
Wenjia Hua and five co-authors revisit Hebbian learning, a training rule inspired by how brain cells wire together. The classic backpropagation rule trains most deep networks, but it is not how brains learn and it costs a lot to run. Hebbian rules are local and cheaper, yet they have lagged in performance.

The authors add a shared global direction to guide the local updates. That signal helps the local rules pull together instead of drifting. The goal is training that stays brain-like but works at modern scale. Success would open cheaper, more brain-like ways to build capable networks.
arxiv-2601-21667:
Hao Ju, Shaofei Huang, Hongyu Li, Zihan Ding, Si Liu, Meng Wang, and Zhedong Zheng let mobile robots act on sounds instead of waiting for commands. Most mobile manipulation research is instruction-driven: a person states a task and the robot obeys. That setup keeps the robot passive, reacting only when told.

Real homes and wards are full of events worth acting on, like a kettle whistling or a glass breaking. The authors trigger robot action from sound, so the robot notices and responds on its own. Event-driven action is a step toward helpers that share awareness of the room, not just obedience to text.
arxiv-2601-22267:
Members of the MicroBooNE team report new measures of how neutrinos hit argon atoms. Their write-up sums up data from a large tank of liquid argon at Fermilab, near Chicago. The tank sat in one beam of neutrinos and near a second beam. It logged a vast set of hits over its run.

Such hit rates are key inputs for planned, larger neutrino hunts. They help teams predict what a future tank will see when a beam passes through. The data also test how well models of these hits match real events. That match shapes the hunt for new physics in neutrino change.
arxiv-2601-22367:
Shiyi Sun, Geoff Nicholls, and Jeong Eun Lee speed up a safe form of Bayesian inference. The generalized form softens the loss with a heat-like dial, which guards against a wrong model. Their 2026 preprint notes that old samplers for it are slow and must restart for each new data set and dial value.

Their method trains a neural net to give the answer at once, for any dial value. Fast, safe inference helps when models are known to be rough. It fits fields from climate to health. The work makes a careful method cheap enough for daily use.
arxiv-2601-21767:
Wei Zhu examines how well ChatGPT handles a practical medical task: pulling structured facts out of clinical text. Large language models can chat fluently and follow user intent, but hospitals and researchers need systems that extract names, conditions, and treatments with care. His 2026 preprint tests ChatGPT on medical information extraction tasks.

The study looks at performance and at explainability, meaning whether the model can show why it gave an answer. It also looks beyond those two points at wider questions about using such models in medicine. Readers get a grounded check on what a general chatbot can and cannot yet do with sensitive clinical language.
arxiv-2601-21967:
Ilche Georgievski, Serhat Tekin, and Marco Aiello measure an overlooked cost of automated planning: electricity. Artificial intelligence research has long prized accuracy and runtime. The Green AI movement argues that energy use is a performance measure too, yet planning has barely been studied this way.

Planning systems search for action sequences that reach a goal, and the domain model describes the world they search in. The team's 2026 preprint, written for a sustainable computing conference, tests how the design of that domain model changes energy use. Two models of the same problem can solve alike but burn very different power. That insight could help engineers write models that are cheaper for both computers and the climate.
arxiv-2601-20867:
Jaehyuk Jang, Wonjun Lee, Kangwook Ko, and Changick Kim study how to tune audio-language models so the skill transfers. Their 2026 paper concerns prompt tuning. The method adjusts a small set of learned prompts instead of the whole model. It worked well for vision-language models and is now used for audio-language models too. Its generalization, though, remains largely unexplored.

The authors spot a base-new trade-off in standard prompt tuning. Gains on known classes come at the cost of new ones. They trace the issue to a disrupted semantic structure in the embedding space. Their fix expands that semantic structure to protect it. The work helps audio models that must greet new sounds without forgetting old ones. It is a careful study of a small method with wide use.
arxiv-2601-20967:
Willy Fischler proposes a search for a subtle cosmic angle using black hole images. His 2026 paper concerns a CP-violating electromagnetic vacuum angle. Such an angle would add a term coupling electric and magnetic fields in empty space. The Event Horizon Telescope images black holes by their glowing rings. Fischler asks whether those images could betray the angle's presence. The targets are Sagittarius A* and M87*.

Sagittarius A* sits at the center of our own galaxy. M87* anchors a giant galaxy nearby. Both have been imaged in fine detail. A vacuum angle might twist the polarization of their light. The paper examines whether that twist is extractable. It is a bold proposal joining particle theory with observation. Even a null result would bound a constant of nature.
arxiv-2512-01467:
Fabian Kresse and Christoph Lampert ask if logic circuits can steer robots. Most control policies are neural nets with smooth weights. Circuits use yes-no gates and lookup tables. They are fast, tiny, and easy to check, but hard to train.

Their design, called DWCs, learns circuits in a smooth way. Real inputs are first coded as thermometer bits. Sparse gate layers then pick actions. The result is a policy made of pure logic. Logic policies could run on cheap chips for drones and tools where nets are too heavy. Circuits also shrug off weight noise, since a gate is right or wrong with no gray zone for small hardware faults to exploit.
arxiv-2512-01567:
Meng Hua and co-authors blend in-context learning with deep joint coding for image sends. Joint source-channel coding sends images over noisy links in one learned step. Over MIMO links, with many antennas, the task gets harder. Channel states shift fast.

Large models can learn from a few examples in context. The team uses that skill to adapt the coder on the fly. Few-shot adaptation avoids retraining for each new channel. Adaptive coding could keep image quality high on mobile links where conditions change by the second. Context examples ride in the signal itself, so the receiver needs no side channel to learn the sender's code for each new image.
arxiv-2512-01667:
Qingyang Liu and co-authors detect model flaws in Bayesian inverse problems. Bayesian inference is optimal when the model fits. When it does not, results can fail badly. Many post-Bayesian fixes have been offered for that risk.

Their method uses variational gradient descent to spot misspecification. Predictively oriented views lift the model itself during checks. A clear flaw alarm lets users fix the model before trusting its answers. That guard matters in imaging and geophysics, where inverse answers guide costly acts. The check runs after fitting, so it guards real workflows where a flawed model has already shaped the data analysis once.
arxiv-2512-01767:
Tsvetana Stoyanova proves non-integrability of the Sasano system of a stated affine type. The system is a four-dimensional nonlinear set of differential equations. It has affine Weyl group symmetries. It is also a time-dependent Hamiltonian system, seen as coupled Painleve III systems.

Non-integrability means no full set of conserved quantities exists. Proving it rules out exact solution by classic means. The result guides scholars to numeric or asymptotic tools for this system. Coupled Painleve systems arise in random matrices and statistical physics. Hamiltonian form sharpens the proof's bite, since integrable Hamiltonian systems are common enough that a ruled-out case saves much wasted search.
arxiv-2512-00867:
Obada Kraishan wrote a 2025 paper on a delicate choice programmers now face: whether to credit AI help. Coding assistants have changed how open-source software gets written. Developers must decide whether to note AI assistance in their commits, while weighing how their community will judge that honesty.

Kraishan calls this the AI attribution paradox and studies it in GitHub data. The analysis covers thousands of repositories and commits across several major AI tools in recent years. It looks at how developers disclose AI use and how communities respond. The findings matter as open-source projects write rules for fair credit.
arxiv-2512-00967:
Sarah Huang and Chen Jiang apply machine learning to planet hunting in a 2025 paper. NASA's Kepler and TESS missions measure starlight with great precision. They have found thousands of confirmed exoplanets by the transit method, where a planet dims its star as it crosses. Many more candidates still await validation.

Confirming a candidate as a real planet takes careful vetting and follow-up observing, which slows discovery in huge datasets. Huang and Jiang use machine learning to validate TESS candidates and to flag planets in the habitable zone, where liquid water could exist. Faster, reliable validation would focus telescope time on the best candidates.
arxiv-2512-01067:
Evan Dramko and six coauthors rethink how atomistic models are fine-tuned in a 2025 paper. Machine-learning interatomic potentials estimate forces between atoms far faster than first-principles physics, enabling structural relaxations that find stable materials. Training them usually means matching computed forces as faithfully as possible.

The authors view fine-tuning through iterated maps, where a relaxation applies the model again and again. Training with backpropagation through time lets the model learn from its own relaxation paths, not just single steps. That lens could produce potentials that stay accurate over long relaxations, which is what materials discovery actually needs.
arxiv-2601-22867:
Peter Oehme looks for faster ways to run Dynamic Mode Decomposition on very large datasets. The method, tied to Koopman operator theory, pulls the main patterns of motion out of snapshots of a system. It is used for fluids, power grids, and other systems that change over time.

For huge data, the standard method can be too slow, so randomized shortcuts are tested. Random sampling can cut the cost while keeping the main patterns intact. Faster pattern-finding means engineers can watch complex systems in near real time. Randomized techniques suit this setting because they trade a little precision for very large savings in time and memory.
arxiv-2601-23267:
Brennan Undseth and a large team demonstrate weight-four parity checks with silicon spin qubits. Semiconductor spin qubits are an appealing platform for quantum processors. Recent coherent spin shuttling gives these arrays dynamic, long-range connectivity.

That connectivity is essential for many quantum error-correction schemes. Parity checks of weight four are a basic building block for detecting errors without reading the data itself. Showing them in silicon brings fault-tolerant quantum computing on chips a step closer. Sparse arrays enabled by shuttling are the platform context, trading dense wiring for movable, long-range qubit connections.
arxiv-2512-00167:
Positive operators are a basic object in functional analysis, the branch of mathematics behind quantum theory. James Tian investigates a way to break such operators into rank-one pieces in a 2025 study. The scheme is iterative, proceeding step by step with weights taken from what remains.

At each step, the operator is compressed along a chosen unit vector while staying inside the positive cone. The update rule defines a monotone dynamical system on that cone. The work is pure mathematics, offering a new process whose long-run behavior may interest operator theorists and mathematical physicists. Rank-one pieces are the simplest operators, so building everything from them is an appealing idea.
arxiv-2512-00267:
False information now spreads online with a single click, which makes automated fact-checking necessary. Anab Maulana Barik and co-authors present Trification in 2025, a tree-based strategy planner for fact-checking with structural verification. Their aim is to protect the safety and integrity of online media.

Earlier methods showed that splitting a claim into simpler sub-tasks helps, with language-model agents carrying them out. Trification organizes that decomposition as a tree and verifies the structure of the check. A more disciplined planning scheme could make automated verdicts easier to audit before they reach readers. Tree structures make each verification step traceable back to the original claim. That traceability is what editors need before publishing an automated verdict.
arxiv-2512-00367:
Retrieval-augmented generation answers questions by first fetching relevant document chunks, so how documents are split matters greatly. Aparajitha Allamraju and co-authors study domain-aware semantic segmentation for this pipeline in 2025. Fixed-length and recursive splitters often cut text at arbitrary, incoherent points.

Semantic chunking has gained traction, but its influence on generation quality remains underexplored. The authors break documents down along domain-aware boundaries so retrieved context stays precise and coherent. Better chunking quietly improves every downstream answer, which makes it a high-leverage piece of practical AI engineering. Chunk quality is invisible when it works and obvious when answers quote the wrong passage. Domain-aware splitting respects the document's own sections instead of counting characters. For teams who build search tools, the lesson is plain. How you cut a text is not a small chore, and the cut shapes each reply the tool can give.
arxiv-2512-03167:
When two theories meet at a surface, energy can cross or bounce. Avik Banerjee and Giuseppe Policastro study that meeting point in this 2025 work. They look at conformal field theories changed by a known deformation, joined by an interface.

Such interfaces show a broad pattern in how much energy passes and how much reflects. The authors examine those shares for the deformed case. Their results add to the theory of defects in quantum systems. That theory helps model wires, junctions, and other sharp joins in physics. Reflection shares guide how energy moves in devices built from joined quantum materials.
arxiv-2512-03367:
A neat correspondence links operators to pairs of simpler objects. Weixi Chen, Mee Seong Im, Mikhail Khovanov, Catherine Lillja, and Nicolas Rugo extend that link in this 2025 work. Tom Leinster gave a bijection between operators on a vector space and certain pairs.

Each pair holds a nilpotent operator and a vector. The authors study pairs of eventually constant maps and nilpotent pairs. Over a finite field, such counts give exact probabilities, like the chance an operator is nilpotent. The work blends algebra and combinatorics in a clean way. Counting over finite fields turns an abstract bijection into exact, testable numbers.
arxiv-2512-03467:
Chronic diseases progress in a few typical patterns, not random ones. Hongtao Hao and Joseph Austerweil present a Bayesian event-based model in this 2025 work. They build on work with the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.

Their model infers disease subtypes and stages from mostly cross-sectional data. It estimates how many subtypes exist, the order of progression for each, and each patient's subtype. Knowing a patient's pattern can guide prognosis and trial design. The method aims to capture structured differences among patients. Subtype labels could refine prognosis, since two patients at one stage may face different futures depending on their progression pattern.
arxiv-2512-02067:
Dark energy drives the cosmos to expand faster and faster. How strong it is hangs on how the growth of structure is counted. Mauro Carfora and Francesca Familiari give in 2025 a shape-based route to that link. They compare lightcones, the full records of all light that can reach one watcher.

Their route skips step-by-step approximations. It lets a standard watcher gauge a distance that shifts with scale and ties to the dark energy share. Such work counts, since the standard model's tale of late-time structure still grates against its dark energy claims. A cleaner gauge could help settle how much of the cosmos is dark energy at all.
arxiv-2512-02267:
Partitions split a whole number into parts. Some chance rules on them tie into growth and random matrix work. Jimmy He and Michael Wheeler study two such rules in 2025. Both have a free edge: the q-Whittaker process and the Hall-Littlewood process.

They prove a neat fact about one gauge of the q-Whittaker rule. After a random shift, that gauge gains a symmetry in two dials at once. The proof broadens past work by Imamura, Mucciconi, and Sasamoto, and a later growth of it by He. Such symmetries are the hinges of this field. They turn one solved case into a spring of exact formulas.
arxiv-2512-02667:
Haozhuo Zheng, Cheng Wang, and Yang Liu generate new molecules with a two stage transformer system. Designing molecules with wanted traits is slow when each candidate must be built and tested. Diffusion models generate well but cost heavy compute, while step by step models can drift into errors.

Their Graph VQ-Transformer first compresses molecules into high fidelity discrete codes. A transformer then writes new codes, which decode into full molecular graphs. The design aims for diffusion level accuracy at lower cost, helping chemists search larger chemical spaces for drugs and materials. Codes that keep the shape of the whole graph keep the traits that make a drug work or fail.
arxiv-2512-03067:
Difu Feng and five co-authors measure how easily a user could escape a recommendation filter bubble. Recommender systems shape what users see by modeling their preferences closely. That strategy reinforces existing tastes, trapping users in filter bubbles linked to group polarization.

Reasonable measures of bubbles are needed before platforms can fix them. Their behavior aware measure uses contrastive simulation to score escape potential. A number for escapability lets platforms compare designs and prove that a change truly widens what users can discover. A score for how stuck a user is turns a vague gripe about feeds into a mark. Shops can be held to that mark when they tune what folks see each day.
plos-pone-0010167:
The authors were Galeb Abu-Ali, Lindsey Ouellette, Scott Henderson, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study compared strains of a dangerous gut bacterium. E. coli O157:H7 spreads through food and water and can cause severe illness. Its strains fall into nine lineages, and one, clade 8, was tied to a serious kidney complication in patients.

The team found that this human-associated lineage sticks to surfaces more strongly. It also expressed its virulence genes at higher levels. Those two traits may explain why this lineage shows up so often in human infections.
plos-pone-0010367:
Swapnalee Sarmah and colleagues showed that a shipping protein is vital for zebrafish bones, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells send proteins out through a relay that starts at an inner factory, the endoplasmic reticulum. Tiny coated carriers, called COPII, ferry cargo on the first leg. Sec24D is one adaptor that picks which cargo rides. The team studied zebrafish mutants, nicknamed bulldog, with a broken adaptor.

Without working Sec24D, matrix proteins for building tissue were not shipped properly. The young fish then formed their skeletons wrongly. The defect links a general shipping job to a specific body outcome. It also offers a model for human bone and cartilage disorders. Sometimes, the authors show, development fails at the loading dock.
plos-pone-0009867:
Cerebral malaria is the deadliest form of malaria, attacking the brain. J. Brian de Souza and colleagues tested whether swallowing activated charcoal could prevent it in mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Activated charcoal soaks up chemicals in the gut and is a standard poison treatment. The mouse results were paired with a randomized controlled trial in people. That trial checked whether charcoal interfered with intravenous artesunate, a key malaria drug. It did not, clearing one safety worry for the idea. The human trial focused on drug levels, not on curing malaria.
plos-pone-0009967:
Dengue can turn severe in children, and blood markers may warn which cases will worsen. Penelope Koraka and colleagues measured one protein family in children with acute dengue. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dengue is spread by mosquitoes in warm regions.

The proteins are inter-alpha inhibitor proteins, measured in plasma, the liquid part of blood. Plasma levels were checked during acute dengue virus infection. Markers that track severity could help doctors watch the riskiest children closely. Dengue threatens millions across the tropics each year. Acute means the illness was in its early, active phase.
